BIB.10.1.1.t: Identify the Ten Commandments as God's rules for living.
Name lying and stealing as wrong.
Recall that we should love our neighbor.
Observe that God sees everything we do.
Summarize the two greatest commandments (Love God, Love Neighbor).
Explain why we tell the truth (because God is Truth).
Compare what the world says is right with what the Bible says.
Apply the Golden Rule to bullying.
Analyze the Sermon on the Mount ethics (anger = murder, lust = adultery).
Interpret the relationship between Law and Grace in ethics.
Connect the value of life (Imago Dei) to issues like abortion.
Explain the Christian view of work and laziness.
Construct a biblical framework for decision making.
Evaluate ethical dilemmas (e.g., war, bioethics) through a scriptural lens.
Defend objective morality against moral relativism.
Synthesize the 'Third Use of the Law' (guide for the believer).

BIB.10.1.2.t: Identify holiness as being like Jesus.
Name sin as the opposite of holiness.
Recall that the Holy Spirit helps us be good.
Observe that God is happy when we obey.
Summarize the command 'Be holy for I am holy'.
Explain the difference between justification (one time) and sanctification (ongoing).
Compare worldly happiness with biblical joy.
Apply the 'put off / put on' principle (Ephesians 4).
Interpret the struggle with the flesh in Romans 7.
Connect holiness to witness (being salt and light).
Explain the Puritan concept of the 'Mortification of Sin' (killing sin).
Construct a personal plan for spiritual growth (Means of Grace).
Evaluate legalism vs. antinomianism in the pursuit of holiness.
Defend the necessity of holiness ('without which no one will see the Lord').
Synthesize the doctrine of Union with Christ as the source of godliness.

BIB.10.1.3.t: Identify prayer as talking to God our Father.
Recall that God always hears us.
Summarize the A.C.T.S. model (Adoration, Confession, Thanksgiving, Supplication).
Explain why we pray 'in Jesus' name'.
Compare private prayer with corporate (group) prayer.
Apply the practice of praying for enemies.
Analyze the prayers of Paul in the Epistles.
Interpret the role of the Holy Spirit in intercession (Romans 8).
Connect prayer to the sovereignty of God (Why pray if God knows?).
Explain the discipline of fasting as an aid to prayer.
Construct a theology of prayer based on the priesthood of believers.
Evaluate the difference between mystical contemplation and biblical meditation.
Defend the effectiveness of prayer against deistic views.
Synthesize the relationship between prayer and providence.

BIB.10.1.4.t: Identify the Fruit of the Spirit as good things God grows in us.
Name Love, Joy, Peace, Patience, Kindness, Goodness, Faithfulness, Gentleness, Self-control.
Recall that a bad tree cannot bear good fruit.
Observe how Jesus showed these fruits.
Explain that we cannot grow this fruit without the Spirit.
Compare the 'Works of the Flesh' with the 'Fruit of the Spirit'.
Apply 'Self-control' to a specific situation (like anger or eating).
Analyze why it is 'Fruit' (singular) and not 'Fruits' (plural).
Interpret the meaning of 'Faithfulness' in a covenant context.
Connect the fruit of the Spirit to the character of Christ.
Construct a study on the Greek term 'Agape' (Love).
Evaluate personal character against the standard of Galatians 5.
Defend the idea that character matters more than gifts.
Produce an essay on how the Spirit produces fruit through abiding (John 15).

BIB.10.2.1.t: Explain the roles of husband and wife (Ephesians 5).
Compare the family to the church.
Analyze marriage as a picture of Christ and the Church.
Interpret the duty to train children in the Lord (Deut 6).
Connect covenant faithfulness to family stability.
Construct a biblical definition of marriage.
Defend the complementarity of male and female.

BIB.10.2.2.t: Name God as the first Worker.
Recall that we take care of the earth.
Observe people helping others through jobs.
Summarize the command to fill and subdue the earth.
Compare working for money vs. working for God.
Analyze the intrinsic value of work.
Interpret 'Do all to the glory of God'.
Connect skills and talents to service.
Construct a theology of work in a fallen world.
Defend the dignity of all honest labor.
Synthesize cultural engagement with the mandate.

BIB.10.2.3.t: Summarize 'The love of money is a root of all kinds of evil'.
Analyze the Parable of the Talents.
Connect generosity to trust in God.
Explain the biblical view of private property (Thou shalt not steal).
Construct a plan for financial stewardship.
Evaluate socialism and capitalism through a biblical lens.
Defend the moral obligation to care for the poor.
Synthesize wealth creation with kingdom purposes.

BIB.10.2.4.t: Name my body as a temple.
Recall that we should use our gifts.
Explain why we shouldn't waste our lives.
Interpret the body as an instrument of righteousness.
Construct a weekly schedule that honors God.
Evaluate the idolatry of health vs. neglect of the body.
Defend the sanctity of the physical self against Gnosticism.

BIB.10.3.1.t: Identify that we worship God how He likes.
Name the Bible as our guide for church.
Recall that Nadab and Abihu offered 'strange fire'.
Explain: Do what is not forbidden (Normative).
Compare a fun service with a holy service.
Analyze the Reformed view of worship.
Connect worship to the glory of God, not entertainment.
Construct a biblical order of service.
Defend the freedom of conscience in worship.

BIB.10.3.2.t: Recall that we do this together.
Observe the reading of the Bible.
Summarize the dialogical nature of worship (God speaks, we respond).
Compare private prayer with corporate prayer.
Analyze the centrality of the Word.
Interpret the function of Confession and Assurance.
Construct a theology of the gathered assembly.
Evaluate the role of music (teaching vs. feeling).
Synthesize the structure of covenant renewal.

BIB.10.3.3.t: Name bread and cup for Communion.
Recall that Jesus told us to do these things.
Observe a baptism or the Lord's Supper.
Compare a sign with the thing signified.
Explain the Passover connection to the Supper.
Construct a defense of Paedobaptism or Credobaptism.
Evaluate the views of Presence (Symbolic, Spiritual, Physical).
Defend the serious nature of the Table (1 Cor 11).
Synthesize the visible words of the Gospel.

BIB.10.3.4.t: Name going to church on Sunday.
Compare 'Me and Jesus' with 'Us and Jesus'.
Analyze the unique blessings of the corporate gathering.
Interpret the church as a body (cannot survive alone).
Connect private piety to public power.
Construct a plan for daily and weekly rhythms.
Defend the physical gathering of believers.
Synthesize personal growth with communal edification.

BIB.11.10.1.t: Identify God as the only true God.
Name God as All-Powerful and All-Knowing.
Recall that God is everywhere at the same time.
Observe that God does not have a body like us (He is Spirit).
Summarize the Incommunicable Attributes (God alone) vs Communicable (We can share).
Explain that God is Infinite and Eternal.
Compare God's holiness with human sinfulness.
Interpret the Immutability of God (He does not change).
Connect God's simplicity (not made of parts) to His unity.
Explain the Impassibility of God (not controlled by emotions).
Construct a theology of the Divine Perfections.
Evaluate Open Theism vs. Classical Theism.
Defend the knowability of God (we can know Him truly but not fully).
Synthesize the Transcendence and Immanence of God.

BIB.11.10.2.t: Identify God as the King of the world.
Name God as the one who decides what happens.
Recall that nothing is an accident to God.
Observe that God takes care of birds and flowers.
Summarize God's Providence (He upholds and governs all things).
Explain that God is in charge of good things and hard things.
Apply trust in God's plan when things go wrong.
Analyze the distinction between God's sovereign will and His moral will.
Interpret Romans 9 ('Jacob I loved, Esau I hated').
Connect divine sovereignty to human responsibility (compatibilism).
Explain the doctrine of Election (choosing) and Predestination.
Construct a theology of the Decrees (God's eternal plan).
Evaluate the Arminian vs. Calvinist view of election.
Defend the goodness of God amidst the reality of evil.
Synthesize the comfort of sovereignty for evangelism and prayer.

BIB.11.10.3.t: Identify God as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
Name the Trinity as Three Persons but One God.
Recall the baptism of Jesus where we see all three.
Observe that we pray to the Father, in Jesus' name, by the Spirit.
Summarize the shield of the Trinity (Father is God, Son is God, Spirit is God).
Explain that there are not three gods (Tritheism).
Compare the Trinity to nothing else (analogies usually fail).
Apply the beauty of the Trinity to God's love (He was never lonely).
Analyze the ontological equality and economic subordination (roles).
Connect the Trinity to the plan of redemption.
Explain the heresy of Modalism (God wearing 'masks').
Construct a defense of the Trinity from the Old Testament.
Evaluate the filioque clause controversy (procession of the Spirit).
Defend the doctrine against Unitarianism and Mormonism.
Produce a reflection on the social Trinity as the model for human relationships.

BIB.11.1.1.t: Identify angels as spirits God created.
Recall that angels are invisible and mighty.
Observe that angels worship God around His throne.
Summarize what angels are (created, spiritual, personal beings).
Explain that angels are created spirits, not glorified humans.
Compare the power of an angel with the power of a human.
Categorize the kinds of angels (cherubim, seraphim, archangels).
Analyze the function of the cherubim as guardians of holiness.
Interpret the 'divine council' (God presiding over spiritual beings).
Connect the multitude of angels to the greatness of God.
Explain the moral state of the holy angels (confirmed in holiness).
Construct a biblical angelology from the whole of Scripture.
Evaluate cultural and sentimental myths about angels.
Defend the reality of the unseen spiritual realm against naturalism.
Synthesize angels as God's mighty servants who do His will.

BIB.11.1.2.t: Identify angels as God's helpers who serve His people.
Name Gabriel, who announced good news to Mary.
Recall that angels obey God and do what He says.
Observe that angels rejoice when a sinner repents.
Summarize the ministry of angels to believers.
Explain how angels carried God's messages in Scripture.
Compare the angels' worship of God with our worship.
Apply comfort that God commands angels to guard His people.
Analyze the role of angels in redemptive history.
Interpret the angels' service at Christ's birth, temptation, and resurrection.
Connect the ministry of angels to the care of the church.
Explain why we do not worship or pray to angels.
Construct a theology of angelic ministry.
Evaluate the practice of praying to guardian angels.
Defend the ministry of angels without exalting them above Christ.
Synthesize angels as ministering spirits sent to serve the heirs of salvation.

BIB.11.1.3.t: Identify that some angels rebelled against God.
Name Satan as the enemy of God and His people.
Recall that Satan is a liar and a deceiver.
Observe that Satan tempted Adam and Eve.
Summarize the fall of the angels who sinned.
Explain that the devil was created good but fell by pride.
Compare Satan's limited power with God's unlimited power.
Apply watchfulness against the devil's schemes.
Analyze the character and works of Satan (accuser, tempter, deceiver).
Interpret God's providence over the fallen angels' rebellion.
Connect the fall of Satan to the temptation and the promise of Genesis 3:15.
Explain that Satan is a creature under God's sovereign limits.
Construct a biblical account of the origin and fall of Satan.
Evaluate popular myths about the devil (a cartoon villain or God's equal).
Defend the reality of a personal, malevolent enemy against skepticism.
Synthesize Satan's rebellion as real and serious, yet wholly under God's rule.

BIB.11.1.4.t: Identify demons as fallen angels who serve Satan.
Name our need to resist the devil.
Recall that Jesus has power over demons.
Observe that our real battle is spiritual, not against people.
Summarize the reality of spiritual warfare.
Explain the armor of God for standing against the devil.
Compare biblical spiritual warfare with superstition and sensationalism.
Apply resisting the devil by submitting to God.
Analyze the devil's tactics (temptation, accusation, deception).
Interpret Jesus' authority over demons in the Gospels.
Connect our victory to the Word, prayer, and the finished work of Christ.
Explain the limits of Satan's and demons' power over believers.
Construct a sober biblical theology of spiritual warfare.
Evaluate both the denial of the demonic and obsession with it.
Defend the believer's security in Christ against fear of the demonic.
Synthesize spiritual warfare as fought and won in the strength of the Lord.

BIB.11.1.5.t: Identify that Jesus is stronger than Satan.
Name the cross as the place Satan was defeated.
Recall God's promise to crush the serpent.
Observe that nothing can separate believers from God's love.
Summarize Christ's victory over the powers at the cross.
Explain how Jesus 'destroyed the works of the devil.'
Compare our weakness with Christ's triumph over evil.
Apply the promise that the devil flees when we resist him.
Analyze the 'already/not yet' of Satan's defeat and final destruction.
Interpret the disarming of the powers in Colossians 2:15.
Connect Christ's kingly rule to His conquering of every enemy.
Explain the believer's assurance against condemnation and accusation.
Construct a theology of Christ's victory over Satan, sin, and death.
Evaluate fear-driven and triumphalist views of the spiritual realm.
Defend the finality of Christ's victory and the certainty of Satan's doom.
Synthesize the gospel as Christ's conquest that secures His people forever.

BIB.11.2.1.t: Identify humans as God's special creation.
Name Adam and Eve as the first people.
Recall that we are made in God's image.
Observe that every person is valuable to God.
Summarize what 'Imago Dei' means (made to mirror God).
Explain the image of God in knowledge, righteousness, and holiness.
Compare humans with the animals (only humans bear God's image).
Apply the dignity of the image to how we treat others.
Analyze the image as reason, morality, relationship, and dominion.
Interpret the marring of the image at the Fall.
Connect the image of God to the sanctity of human life.
Explain how the image is being renewed in Christ.
Construct a biblical anthropology of the image of God.
Evaluate reductionist views of humanity (materialism, mere animals).
Defend human dignity grounded in the image, not in usefulness.
Synthesize the image of God as created, marred, and restored in Christ.

BIB.11.2.2.t: Identify that a person has a body and a soul.
Name the soul as the part that lives on after death.
Recall that God formed the body from dust and gave it life.
Observe that God cares about both our body and our soul.
Summarize humanity as an embodied soul (material and immaterial).
Explain that the body is good, not evil.
Compare the intermediate state (soul with Christ) and the resurrection (body raised).
Apply the call to glorify God in the body.
Interpret 'spirit and soul and body' in 1 Thessalonians 5:23.
Connect the soul's immortality to the hope of resurrection.
Explain the question of the soul's origin (creationism vs. traducianism).
Construct a theology of the whole person, body and soul.
Evaluate materialism and gnostic dualism as errors.
Defend the goodness of the body against body-denying spiritualities.
Synthesize the redemption of the whole person, soul and body, in Christ.

BIB.11.2.3.t: Identify that God made people male and female.
Name Adam and Eve as man and woman.
Recall that boys and girls are both made in God's image.
Observe that God called His design 'very good.'
Summarize the creation of male and female.
Explain marriage as one man and one woman for life.
Compare complementary design with mere sameness.
Apply respect for both men and women as image-bearers.
Analyze the creation order and its purposes (companionship, procreation).
Interpret Jesus' appeal to 'from the beginning' on marriage.
Connect male and female to the covenant of marriage and family.
Explain marriage as a picture of Christ and the church.
Construct a biblical theology of sex and gender rooted in creation.
Evaluate cultural redefinitions of gender and marriage against creation.
Defend the goodness of God's design with both truth and compassion.
Synthesize creation, distortion, and redemption of manhood and womanhood.

BIB.11.2.4.t: Identify that God gave people work to do.
Name the command to fill the earth and care for it.
Recall that Adam was to tend the garden.
Observe that work is a gift, given before the Fall.
Summarize the Cultural Mandate (be fruitful, fill, subdue, have dominion).
Explain dominion as stewardship, not exploitation.
Compare work before the Fall with work after the Fall (toil).
Apply the calling to do all work 'as unto the Lord.'
Analyze vocation as a sphere of serving God and neighbor.
Interpret the dominion mandate in light of creation care.
Connect the Cultural Mandate to the Great Commission.
Explain the dignity of ordinary work and callings.
Construct a theology of work and vocation from creation.
Evaluate views that treat 'secular' work as less holy than 'sacred' work.
Defend stewardship of creation against both exploitation and nature-worship.
Synthesize labor, rest, and dominion as worship of the Creator.

BIB.11.2.5.t: Identify that Adam and Eve first lived without sin.
Name the one rule God gave in the garden.
Recall that God warned that disobedience would bring death.
Observe that Adam and Eve were good and upright at first.
Summarize the covenant of works (life promised upon perfect obedience).
Explain original righteousness (created in true knowledge and holiness).
Compare the covenant of works with the covenant of grace.
Apply how the broken covenant of works shows our need of Christ.
Analyze Adam as the covenant head of humanity.
Interpret the 'tree of life' and 'tree of knowledge' as covenant signs.
Connect the covenant of works to Christ, the last Adam who kept it.
Explain how Christ's active obedience fulfills what Adam failed.
Construct a theology of the covenant of works.
Evaluate denials of a pre-Fall covenant.
Defend the imputation of Adam's guilt as parallel to Christ's righteousness.
Synthesize the two covenant heads: ruin in Adam, righteousness in Christ.

BIB.11.2.6.t: Identify that every human life is precious to God.
Name people as made in God's image, so life is sacred.
Recall the command 'You shall not murder.'
Observe that God knits us together before birth.
Summarize why human life is sacred (the image of God).
Explain the sixth commandment's protection of life.
Compare the biblical value of life with cultures that devalue it.
Apply the sanctity of life to caring for the weak and vulnerable.
Analyze the personhood of the unborn from Scripture.
Interpret the sixth commandment as forbidding hatred, not just killing.
Connect the image of God to opposition to abortion and euthanasia.
Explain the duties required in the sixth commandment (preserving life).
Construct a pro-life ethic rooted in the imago Dei.
Evaluate arguments for abortion and euthanasia against Scripture.
Defend the dignity of the disabled, aged, and unborn as image-bearers.
Synthesize a Christian ethic of life from creation to resurrection.

BIB.11.3.1.t: Identify that there are 66 books in the Bible.
Name the Old and New Testaments.
Recall that the church didn't make the Bible, God did.
Observe that we need help to understand hard parts.
Summarize how the books were chosen (Apostles, Truth, Usage).
Explain the 'Perspicuity' (Clarity) of Scripture for salvation.
Compare the Apocrypha with the Canon.
Apply the rule of context when reading a verse.
Interpret the sufficiency of Scripture (we don't need new revelations).
Connect the closing of the canon to the death of the Apostles.
Explain the role of the Holy Spirit in interpretation.
Construct a history of the canon (Muratorian fragment, councils).
Evaluate the claims of Gnostic gospels.
Defend the closed canon against modern claims of prophecy.
Synthesize the 'Analogy of Faith' (Scripture interprets Scripture).

BIB.11.3.2.t: Name the Bible as the book that is never wrong.
Recall that we must obey what God says.
Observe that Jesus trusted the Bible.
Summarize the definition of 'Inerrancy' (no errors in the original).
Explain that the Bible has authority over our feelings.
Apply the authority of Scripture to a moral choice.
Analyze the Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy (summarized).
Interpret how the Bible can use ordinary language (e.g., sunrise) and still be true.
Connect the authority of the Word to the Lordship of Christ.
Explain the difference between errors and textual variants.
Construct an argument for Inerrancy based on the character of God.
Evaluate common objections to biblical reliability.
Defend the concept of Sola Scriptura (Scripture alone is the highest authority).
Produce an essay on the relationship between Church authority and Biblical authority.

BIB.11.3.3.t: Identify the Bible as God's special letter to us.
Name the Bible as the only book that is perfectly true.
Recall that God 'breathed' out the words of Scripture.
Observe that we need the Bible to know who Jesus is.
Summarize what 'Inspiration' means (God used men to write His words).
Explain why we need the Bible (General Revelation isn't enough to save).
Compare the Bible with other good books (the Bible is the boss).
Apply the truth that Scripture is useful for teaching and correcting.
Analyze the concept of 'Verbal Plenary Inspiration'.
Connect the necessity of Scripture to our inability to find God on our own.
Explain the distinction between Revelation and Illumination.
Construct a defense of the Bible's divine origin.
Evaluate the 'Neo-orthodox' view of inspiration vs. the orthodox view.
Defend the necessity of special revelation for salvation.
Synthesize the dual authorship of Scripture (100% God, 100% Man).

BIB.11.4.1.t: Identify Jesus as God the Son.
Name Jesus as the One who made all things.
Recall that Jesus existed before He was born in Bethlehem.
Observe that people rightly worshiped Jesus.
Summarize Jesus' words, 'Before Abraham was, I AM.'
Explain that the Word was with God and was God.
Compare the Son's eternity with created things (He was not made).
Categorize the titles of Christ's deity (Lord, I AM, Son of God, Word).
Analyze the 'I AM' statements in the Gospel of John.
Interpret the eternal generation of the Son (begotten, not made).
Connect Old Testament theophanies to the preincarnate Son.
Explain the Son as the agent of creation and providence.
Construct a biblical case for the full deity of Christ.
Evaluate the Arian claim that 'there was when the Son was not.'
Defend the worship of Christ as proper to God alone.
Synthesize the homoousios ('of one substance') of Nicaea.

BIB.11.4.2.t: Identify that God the Son became a real human being.
Name Jesus as both God and man.
Recall that the baby Jesus was born of Mary.
Observe that Jesus grew, got tired, and got hungry like us.
Compare Jesus' two natures without mixing them together.
Categorize what belongs to His deity and what to His humanity.
Analyze the virgin conception by the Holy Spirit.
Interpret morphe ('form of God' / 'form of a servant') in Philippians 2.
Connect the incarnation to why the Mediator had to be both God and man.
Explain the hypostatic union: two natures in one person.
Construct the Chalcedonian formula ('without confusion, change, division, or separation').
Evaluate the heresies it excludes (Nestorianism, Eutychianism, Apollinarianism).
Defend the sinlessness and impeccability of Christ.
Synthesize the communicatio idiomatum (the properties of both natures ascribed to the one person).

BIB.11.4.3.t: Identify that Jesus came down low to save us.
Name that Jesus was born poor, in a manger.
Recall that Jesus obeyed His parents and His Father.
Observe that Jesus suffered and died on the cross.
Summarize Christ's humiliation (born low, made under the law, died, buried).
Explain that Jesus 'emptied Himself' and took the form of a servant.
Compare the humiliation with the exaltation of Christ.
Apply the humility of Christ to how we serve others.
Analyze the kenosis as what Christ veiled, not what He surrendered.
Interpret 'He descended' and 'continued under the power of death.'
Connect His obedience 'unto death' to the covenant of redemption.
Explain the four steps of exaltation (resurrection, ascension, session, return).
Construct the two-states framework of Christ's saving work.
Evaluate erroneous kenotic theories (that the Son gave up divine attributes).
Defend the bodily resurrection as the vindication of the humiliated Christ.
Synthesize how humiliation and exaltation together accomplish redemption.

BIB.11.4.4.t: Identify Jesus as our Prophet, Priest, and King.
Name Jesus as the Good Shepherd who leads us.
Recall that Jesus teaches us the truth about God.
Observe that Jesus prays for His people.
Summarize the meaning of 'Christ' (the Anointed One).
Explain Jesus as the Prophet greater than Moses.
Compare the three offices and the need each one meets.
Categorize Christ's priestly work as sacrifice and intercession.
Analyze Christ as High Priest after the order of Melchizedek.
Interpret Christ's kingly rule over His church and all things.
Connect the offices to the Old Testament anointing of prophets, priests, and kings.
Explain how Christ executes each office in both humiliation and exaltation.
Construct a theology of Christ's ongoing intercession.
Evaluate the error of reducing Christ to only teacher or only king.
Defend the sufficiency and finality of Christ's priesthood.
Synthesize the mediatorial work of Christ as our only Redeemer.

BIB.11.4.5.t: Identify that Jesus died to take away our sin.
Name Jesus as the Lamb of God.
Recall that Jesus took the punishment we deserved.
Observe that Jesus shed His blood for us.
Summarize substitution: Christ died in our place.
Explain propitiation (Christ turning away God's wrath).
Compare the Old Testament sacrifices with Christ's once-for-all sacrifice.
Apply the cross to the assurance of forgiveness.
Analyze the necessity of the atonement (why God could not simply overlook sin).
Connect Christ's active and passive obedience to our justification.
Explain expiation and reconciliation as effects of the cross.
Construct a defense of the definite (particular) extent of the atonement.
Evaluate governmental and moral-influence theories against penal substitution.
Defend the justice and love of God meeting at the cross.
Synthesize the atonement as the satisfaction of divine justice.

BIB.11.4.6.t: Identify that Jesus rose from the dead.
Name Easter as the day Jesus came alive again.
Recall that Jesus went up into heaven.
Observe that Jesus is alive and reigning right now.
Summarize the bodily resurrection on the third day.
Explain the ascension (taken up in the sight of the disciples).
Compare the empty tomb with the claims raised against it.
Apply the hope of resurrection to the believer's own future.
Analyze the resurrection as the 'firstfruits' guaranteeing ours.
Interpret Christ's session at the right hand (Psalm 110:1).
Connect the session to Christ's continual intercession for us.
Explain Christ's present kingly rule from the right hand of God.
Construct a case for the resurrection as a historical event.
Evaluate naturalistic theories that deny the resurrection.
Defend the necessity of the resurrection for our justification.
Synthesize resurrection, ascension, and session as Christ's exaltation and our hope.

BIB.11.5.1.t: Identify the Church as God's people, not a building.
Name believers together as the family of God.
Recall that Jesus builds His church.
Observe that Christians gather to worship and love one another.
Summarize the church as the body of Christ.
Explain the visible and the invisible church.
Compare the local church with the universal (catholic) church.
Apply the call to belong to and love the church.
Analyze the biblical images of the church (body, bride, temple, flock).
Interpret the church as the covenant people of God.
Connect the church to union with Christ its head.
Explain the communion of the saints.
Construct a theology of the church as visible and invisible.
Evaluate individualism ('just me and Jesus') against the biblical church.
Defend the necessity of the church in the Christian life.
Synthesize the church as the people Christ gathers, defends, and preserves.

BIB.11.5.2.t: Identify that a true church teaches God's Word.
Name the Bible as the church's authority.
Recall the creed's four words: one, holy, catholic, apostolic.
Observe that a church preaches, baptizes, and shares the Lord's Supper.
Summarize the marks of a true church (Word, sacraments, discipline).
Explain the notes of the church: right preaching and right sacraments.
Compare a faithful church with a false or apostate church.
Apply discernment in recognizing a healthy church.
Analyze the four attributes (unity, holiness, catholicity, apostolicity).
Interpret 'one holy catholic and apostolic church.'
Connect church discipline to the church's purity.
Explain that even the purest churches have mixture and error.
Construct a theology of the marks of a true church.
Evaluate claims that one denomination alone is 'the true church.'
Defend the necessity of doctrine, ordinances, and discipline together.
Synthesize the marks and attributes as signs of Christ's true church.

BIB.11.5.3.t: Identify that Christ is the Head of the church.
Name pastors and elders who shepherd the church.
Recall that deacons serve the church's needs.
Observe that leaders are to be godly examples.
Summarize the two offices: elders (oversight) and deacons (service).
Explain the qualifications for elders and deacons.
Compare the roles of elders (teach and lead) and deacons (serve).
Apply submission to and prayer for church leaders.
Analyze Christ's rule through the keys of the kingdom.
Interpret the exercise of church discipline.
Connect the ministry of the Word to the calling of qualified men.
Explain the purposes of church discipline (restoration, purity, witness).
Construct a case for a particular form of church government.
Evaluate episcopal, presbyterian, and congregational polities.
Defend biblical eldership and the plurality of elders.
Synthesize Christ's kingly rule through Word, officers, and censures.

BIB.11.5.4.t: Identify baptism and the Lord's Supper as gifts from Jesus.
Name water, bread, and wine as the outward signs.
Recall that Jesus told us to baptize and to remember Him in the Supper.
Observe that the sacraments point us to Christ.
Summarize a sacrament as a sign and seal of the covenant of grace.
Explain the meaning of baptism (union with Christ, cleansing).
Compare baptism (once, initiation) with the Lord's Supper (often, nourishment).
Apply self-examination before the Lord's Supper.
Analyze what the Lord's Supper is (showing forth Christ's death, spiritual feeding).
Interpret the presence of Christ in the Supper (spiritual, received by faith).
Connect the sacraments to the covenant and the church.
Explain worthy versus unworthy receiving of the Supper.
Construct a theology of the sacraments as means of grace.
Evaluate transubstantiation and bare memorialism against the Reformed view.
Defend the Reformed understanding of the sacraments as signs and seals.
Synthesize baptism and the Supper as visible words of the gospel.

BIB.11.5.5.t: Identify that God tells us how to worship Him.
Name reading the Bible, prayer, singing, and preaching as worship.
Recall that we worship God, not idols.
Observe that God wants worship from the heart.
Summarize worship 'in spirit and in truth.'
Explain the elements of worship God has commanded.
Compare the regulative principle with the normative principle.
Apply reverence and joy in corporate worship.
Analyze what God commands versus what He forbids in worship.
Interpret the second commandment's regulation of worship.
Connect the Lord's Day to the pattern of Christian worship.
Explain the elements of worship (Word, sacraments, prayer, praise, giving).
Construct a defense of the regulative principle of worship.
Defend God-centered worship against man-centered innovation.
Synthesize worship as glorifying God as He commands.

BIB.11.5.6.t: Identify that Jesus sends His church to make disciples.
Name sharing the gospel as the church's task.
Recall Jesus' promise to be with us always.
Observe that the good news is for all nations.
Summarize the Great Commission (make disciples, baptize, teach).
Explain the church as a witness to the ends of the earth.
Compare evangelism (proclaiming) with discipleship (teaching to obey).
Apply your part in the church's mission (pray, give, go, send).
Analyze the marks of the missionary church in Acts.
Interpret the relationship of Word and deed in mission.
Connect the Great Commission to the reign of the risen Christ.
Explain the church's mission as gospel proclamation, not merely social action.
Construct a biblical theology of missions from Genesis to Revelation.
Evaluate the prosperity gospel and social gospel against the true gospel.
Defend the exclusivity of the gospel and the necessity of missions.
Synthesize the church's mission as making disciples of all nations for God's glory.

BIB.11.6.1.t: Identify that everyone will die one day.
Name that believers go to be with Jesus when they die.
Recall that death is not the end for God's people.
Observe that Jesus took away the sting of death.
Summarize what happens to believers at death (souls made perfect, with Christ).
Explain the intermediate state (the soul between death and resurrection).
Compare the believer's death with the unbeliever's death.
Apply the comfort of 'to depart and be with Christ.'
Analyze the state of the soul apart from the body until the resurrection.
Interpret Jesus' words to the thief, 'Today you will be with me in Paradise.'
Connect the intermediate state to the future resurrection of the body.
Explain why the intermediate state is not the final hope (the body will rise).
Construct a theology of death and the intermediate state.
Evaluate soul sleep and purgatory against Scripture.
Defend conscious existence with Christ after death.
Synthesize the believer's hope in death: absent from the body, present with the Lord.

BIB.11.6.2.t: Identify that Jesus is coming back.
Name Jesus as the King who will return.
Recall the angels' promise that Jesus will come again.
Observe that we should watch and be ready.
Summarize the Second Coming of Christ.
Explain that Christ will return visibly and personally.
Compare Christ's first coming (in humility) with His second (in glory).
Apply the call to live holy lives in light of His return.
Analyze the signs that precede Christ's coming.
Interpret 'no one knows the day or hour.'
Connect the return of Christ to the believer's blessed hope.
Explain the comfort of Christ's return for the suffering church.
Construct a theology of the Second Coming.
Evaluate the danger of date-setting and false predictions.
Defend the personal, bodily, visible return against a merely 'spiritual' coming.
Synthesize the return of Christ as judge and redeemer, our blessed hope.

BIB.11.6.3.t: Identify that God will raise the dead.
Name the day when Jesus will judge everyone.
Recall that our bodies will be raised.
Observe that everyone will stand before God.
Summarize the general resurrection of the just and the unjust.
Explain the believer's glorified, resurrection body.
Compare the resurrection of the just (to honor) with the unjust (to dishonor).
Apply the hope of resurrection to present grief and suffering.
Analyze the final judgment (its judge, its subjects, and its standard).
Interpret the separation of the sheep and the goats.
Connect the resurrection of Christ to the resurrection of believers.
Explain the purpose of the last judgment (to display God's justice and mercy).
Construct a theology of the resurrection and final judgment.
Evaluate views that deny a bodily resurrection or a final judgment.
Defend the justice of God in the final judgment.
Synthesize resurrection and judgment as the vindication of God and His people.

BIB.11.6.4.t: Identify heaven as being with God forever.
Name the promise of no more tears, death, or pain.
Recall that Jesus is preparing a place for His people.
Observe that the new creation is even better than Eden.
Summarize the new heavens and new earth.
Explain the final state as God dwelling with His people.
Compare the present creation with the renewed creation.
Apply the hope of heaven to how we live now.
Analyze continuity and renewal in the new creation.
Interpret the New Jerusalem as the fulfillment of the temple.
Connect the beatific vision (seeing God) to our final blessedness.
Explain the believer's eternal reward and rest.
Construct a biblical theology of the new creation from Genesis to Revelation.
Evaluate popular but unbiblical pictures of heaven.
Defend the physical, embodied hope of the resurrection life.
Synthesize the new creation as the goal of redemption: God all in all.

BIB.11.6.5.t: Identify that there is a real judgment for sin.
Name hell as separation from God.
Recall that sin against God is serious.
Observe that Jesus Himself warned about hell.
Explain hell as the just penalty for sin against a holy God.
Compare eternal life and eternal punishment in Matthew 25.
Apply the urgency of the gospel in light of judgment.
Analyze the biblical language of hell (fire, darkness, separation).
Connect the justice of hell to the holiness of God.
Explain the final judgment of the wicked.
Construct a careful biblical case for the reality of hell.
Evaluate annihilationism and universalism against Scripture.
Defend the justice of eternal punishment with sobriety and compassion.
Synthesize divine justice and mercy displayed at the last judgment.

BIB.11.6.6.t: Identify that Jesus will reign as King.
Name the 'thousand years' spoken of in Revelation 20.
Recall that God's kingdom will have no end.
Observe that faithful reading handles prophecy with care.
Explain the difference between literal and symbolic reading of Revelation.
Compare premillennial, postmillennial, and amillennial views.
Apply humility and charity in debated matters of prophecy.
Analyze the binding of Satan and the reign of the saints in Revelation 20.
Interpret prophetic and apocalyptic literature according to its genre.
Connect the 'already / not yet' of the kingdom to eschatology.
Explain the relationship of Israel and the church in prophecy.
Construct a careful position on the millennium from the whole of Scripture.
Evaluate sensational 'end-times' schemes and newspaper exegesis.
Defend the certainty of Christ's victory amid differing millennial views.
Synthesize a Christ-centered, hope-filled eschatology that guards the church's unity.

BIB.11.7.1.t: Identify that the first people disobeyed God.
Name Adam and Eve as the first to sin.
Recall that the serpent tempted Eve to doubt God.
Observe that sin entered a good world God had made.
Summarize the Fall (our first parents fell by eating the forbidden fruit).
Explain the covenant of works and its threat of death.
Compare the world before and after the Fall.
Apply how temptation still works (doubt, desire, disobedience).
Analyze the first sin as unbelief and pride.
Interpret the serpent's strategy against God's word.
Connect Satan's role to the origin of temptation.
Explain why God is not the author of sin.
Construct a theology of the Fall from Genesis 3.
Evaluate views that treat Genesis 3 as mere myth.
Defend the historicity of the Fall as essential to the gospel.
Synthesize the Fall as the entry of sin and death, with the first promise of a Redeemer.

BIB.11.7.2.t: Identify that everyone is born with a bent toward sin.
Name Adam as the head who represented all people.
Recall that sin spread to the whole human race.
Observe that even little children need a new heart.
Summarize original sin (guilt, lost righteousness, and a corrupt nature).
Explain federal headship (Adam stood for all his posterity).
Compare being born in sin with committing actual sins.
Apply why we all need Christ, the second Adam.
Analyze the imputation of Adam's guilt to his posterity.
Interpret the transmission of a corrupt nature 'by ordinary generation.'
Connect Adam's headship to Christ's representative work.
Explain the difference between imputed guilt and inherited corruption.
Construct a theology of original sin from Romans 5.
Evaluate Pelagian and semi-Pelagian denials of original sin.
Defend the justice of Adam's headship over the race.
Synthesize the two Adams: condemnation in one, righteousness in the other.

BIB.11.7.3.t: Identify that sin affects every part of us.
Name our natural condition as 'dead in sin.'
Recall that no one is good enough to save himself.
Observe that our hearts naturally turn away from God.
Summarize total depravity (every faculty corrupted, though not as bad as possible).
Explain that the natural person cannot please God.
Compare being 'sick' in sin with being 'dead' in sin.
Apply why salvation must be entirely of grace.
Analyze the bondage of the will apart from grace.
Interpret 'the heart is deceitful above all things.'
Connect spiritual death to the inability to come to Christ unaided.
Explain the noetic effects of sin (how it darkens the mind).
Construct a theology of human inability.
Evaluate free-will theologies against total depravity.
Defend the doctrine of depravity against 'people are basically good.'
Synthesize total depravity as the dark backdrop that magnifies grace.

BIB.11.7.4.t: Identify sin as disobeying God's law.
Name breaking God's commandments as sin.
Recall that everyone sins in what they do and fail to do.
Observe that sin can be in our words, deeds, and thoughts.
Summarize sin as lawlessness (any want of conformity to God's law).
Explain the difference between sins of commission and omission.
Compare outward acts of sin with the sin of the heart.
Apply the tenth commandment's exposure of inward sin (coveting).
Analyze how breaking one command makes us guilty of all.
Interpret Jesus' deepening of the law in the Sermon on the Mount.
Connect actual sins to the corrupt nature that produces them.
Explain that sin is ultimately against God Himself.
Construct a biblical taxonomy of sin (thought, word, deed; commission, omission).
Evaluate the idea that some sins are 'too small to matter.'
Defend the seriousness of sin against a trivializing culture.
Synthesize the law as the mirror that reveals our sin.

BIB.11.7.5.t: Identify that sin separates us from God.
Name death as the result of sin.
Recall that sin makes us guilty before God.
Observe that sin brings sorrow and brokenness into the world.
Summarize the misery of the fallen estate (loss of communion, wrath, and curse).
Explain the guilt and pollution that every sin brings.
Compare temporal, spiritual, and eternal death.
Apply the seriousness of sin to the need for the cross.
Analyze the wrath of God revealed against sin.
Interpret the inward and outward punishments of sin.
Connect physical death to sin's entrance into the world.
Explain the reality of hell as the just penalty for sin.
Construct a theology of sin's fourfold consequence (guilt, corruption, death, wrath).
Evaluate universalism and annihilationism against biblical judgment.
Defend the justice of eternal punishment for sin against a holy God.
Synthesize how sin's consequences drive us to Christ the Redeemer.

BIB.11.7.6.t: Identify that all people everywhere have sinned.
Name the whole world as guilty before God.
Recall that no one is without sin.
Observe that even our best deeds are stained by sin.
Summarize the universality of sin (Jew and Gentile alike).
Explain why every sin deserves God's wrath and curse.
Compare the guilt of different sins (some more heinous than others).
Apply the truth that no sinner can stand on his own merit.
Analyze the aggravations that make some sins more heinous.
Interpret the sin against the Holy Spirit (the unpardonable sin).
Connect the gravity of sin to the infinite worth of the One offended.
Explain that no sin is too great for the truly repentant to be pardoned.
Construct a theology of the gravity of sin before a holy God.
Evaluate the cultural minimizing of sin ('no harm done').
Defend the biblical scale of sin without denying universal guilt.
Synthesize universal guilt and varied gravity as the ground for the gospel offered to all.

BIB.11.8.1.t: Identify the Holy Spirit as God.
Name the Spirit as a Person, not a force.
Recall that the Spirit can be grieved (He is personal).
Observe the Spirit at Jesus' baptism with the Father and the Son.
Summarize the Spirit as the third Person of the Trinity.
Explain that lying to the Spirit is lying to God.
Compare the Spirit's personal acts (teaches, wills, intercedes) with an impersonal force.
Categorize the divine attributes ascribed to the Spirit (eternal, omniscient).
Analyze the Spirit's deity from Acts 5 and 1 Corinthians 2.
Interpret the procession of the Spirit from the Father (and the Son).
Connect the Spirit's Godhead to the baptismal formula and the apostolic benediction.
Explain why the Spirit is worshiped as God.
Construct a defense of the Spirit's deity from Scripture.
Evaluate the error of treating the Spirit as an impersonal power.
Defend the personhood of the Spirit against modalism and subordinationism.
Synthesize the Spirit as true and coeternal God with the Father and the Son.

BIB.11.8.2.t: Identify the Spirit at work in creation.
Name the Spirit as the One who gave us the Bible.
Recall that the Spirit helped the prophets speak God's words.
Observe that the Spirit gives life.
Summarize the Spirit's role in inspiring Scripture.
Explain how the Spirit guides believers into truth.
Compare inspiration (giving the Word) with illumination (understanding the Word).
Apply dependence on the Spirit when reading the Bible.
Analyze the Spirit's inward witness to the Scriptures.
Interpret 'men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.'
Connect the Spirit's inspiration to the authority and inerrancy of the Word.
Explain the internal testimony of the Spirit that confirms Scripture.
Construct a theology of the Spirit's work in creation, providence, and revelation.
Evaluate claims of new revelation against the Spirit's completed inscripturation.
Defend the Spirit as the ultimate Author of Scripture.
Synthesize the Spirit's testimony as the ground of our certainty of God's Word.

BIB.11.8.3.t: Identify the Spirit as the One who gives new life.
Name the Spirit as the Helper who lives in believers.
Recall that believers are 'born of the Spirit.'
Observe that the Spirit points us to Jesus.
Summarize regeneration as the new birth by the Spirit.
Explain what it means that the Spirit indwells the believer.
Compare the person 'in the flesh' with the person 'in the Spirit.'
Apply the truth that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit.
Analyze the Spirit as the One who unites us to Christ.
Interpret the Spirit's work of applying Christ's redemption.
Connect regeneration to effectual calling and faith.
Explain the Spirit's baptism of believers into the body of Christ.
Construct a theology of the Spirit's indwelling and the assurance it brings.
Evaluate the 'second blessing' view of Spirit-baptism against conversion-baptism.
Defend the necessity of the Spirit's regenerating work for salvation.
Synthesize the Spirit as the One who applies to us the redemption purchased by Christ.

BIB.11.8.4.t: Identify the Spirit as our helper to grow in holiness.
Name the fruit of the Spirit.
Recall that the Spirit helps us pray.
Observe that the Spirit makes us more like Jesus.
Summarize walking by the Spirit versus the flesh.
Explain the fruit of the Spirit as the Spirit's work in us.
Apply the call to 'keep in step with the Spirit.'
Analyze the Spirit's inward witness of adoption.
Interpret the Spirit's intercession for us 'with groanings.'
Connect the Spirit's sealing to the believer's assurance and security.
Explain how the Spirit produces assurance without extraordinary revelation.
Construct a theology of the Spirit's role in progressive sanctification.
Evaluate perfectionist claims about the Spirit-filled life.
Defend the Spirit's witness as a ground of assurance alongside the Word.
Synthesize the Spirit as the Seal and Guarantee of our final redemption.

BIB.11.8.5.t: Identify that the Spirit gives gifts to God's people.
Name some gifts of the Spirit (teaching, serving, giving).
Recall that gifts are given to help the whole church.
Observe that the Spirit gives different gifts to different people.
Summarize the purpose of gifts: to build up the body of Christ.
Explain that love is greater than any gift.
Compare the 'sign' gifts with the 'serving' and 'speaking' gifts.
Apply the call to use your gift for others, not for pride.
Analyze the foundational role of apostles and prophets.
Interpret 'when the perfect comes' in 1 Corinthians 13.
Connect the sufficiency of Scripture to the cessationist argument.
Explain the continuationist case for ongoing gifts.
Construct a careful position on the cessationist/continuationist debate.
Evaluate abuses of the gifts (Corinthian disorder, prosperity claims).
Defend the sufficiency of Scripture against claims of authoritative new revelation.
Synthesize the unity of the body amid the diversity of gifts.

BIB.11.9.1.t: Identify that God chose His people before the world began.
Name God's choosing of us as a gift of His love.
Recall that salvation begins with God, not with us.
Observe that God knew us before we were born.
Summarize election (God's free choice of a people in Christ).
Explain predestination 'unto the adoption of sons.'
Compare election by grace with being chosen for works.
Apply the comfort that our salvation rests on God's choice.
Analyze unconditional election (not grounded in foreseen faith).
Interpret 'Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.'
Connect election to the eternal covenant of redemption.
Explain the decree of reprobation with care and reverence.
Construct the 'golden chain' from foreknowledge to glory.
Evaluate Arminian conditional election against the Reformed view.
Defend the justice and freedom of God in election.
Synthesize election as grounds for humility, assurance, and mission.

BIB.11.9.2.t: Identify that God gives His people a new heart.
Name being 'born again' as God's work in us.
Recall that we cannot save ourselves.
Observe that the Spirit moves like the wind, as He wills.
Explain effectual calling (God savingly draws His people).
Compare the outward call of the gospel with the inward effectual call.
Apply the truth that God must open the heart, as He opened Lydia's.
Analyze regeneration as monergistic (God's work alone).
Interpret being made 'alive together with Christ.'
Connect regeneration to the sovereign work of the Spirit.
Explain why regeneration must precede faith.
Construct a theology of effectual calling from Romans 8.
Evaluate decisional regeneration against sovereign regeneration.
Defend the necessity of the new birth to see the kingdom.
Synthesize calling and regeneration as the start of the ordo salutis.

BIB.11.9.3.t: Name repentance as turning away from sin.
Recall that we are saved by believing, not by earning.
Observe that faith and turning from sin go together.
Summarize saving faith (knowledge, assent, and trust).
Explain repentance unto life (godly sorrow that turns to God).
Compare true saving faith with mere intellectual belief.
Apply the call to 'repent and believe the gospel.'
Analyze faith and repentance as two sides of one conversion.
Interpret faith as resting on Christ alone, not on itself.
Connect saving faith to the gift and work of the Spirit.
Explain that faith is a gift, not a meritorious work.
Construct the relationship of faith to justification.
Evaluate easy-believism and works-righteousness as distortions.
Defend the instrumental (not meritorious) role of faith.
Synthesize conversion as the sinner's Spirit-wrought response to grace.

BIB.11.9.4.t: Identify that God declares believers 'not guilty.'
Name Jesus as the One who makes us right with God.
Recall that we are forgiven because of Jesus, not our works.
Observe that Jesus' righteousness is counted as ours.
Explain justification as a legal declaration, 'just as if I had never sinned.'
Compare justification (a declaration) with sanctification (a process).
Apply the peace that comes from being justified.
Analyze the double imputation (our sin to Christ, His righteousness to us).
Interpret justification 'by faith apart from works of the law.'
Connect the ground of justification to Christ's active and passive obedience.
Explain faith as the instrument, not the ground, of justification.
Construct a defense of sola fide from Romans and Galatians.
Evaluate the infused-righteousness view against imputation.
Defend forensic justification against the 'faith plus works' error.
Synthesize justification as the article on which the church stands or falls.

BIB.11.9.5.t: Identify that God makes believers His own children.
Name God as our Father in heaven.
Recall that we may call God 'Abba, Father.'
Observe that God's children are loved and cared for.
Summarize adoption (being received into God's family).
Explain the 'Spirit of adoption' who assures us we are God's.
Compare being a servant with being a son and heir.
Apply the confidence to come to God as Father in prayer.
Analyze adoption as distinct from justification and regeneration.
Interpret believers as 'heirs of God and joint-heirs with Christ.'
Connect adoption to union with the eternal Son.
Explain the privileges and fatherly discipline of God's children.
Construct a theology of adoption from Galatians 4.
Evaluate the 'universal fatherhood of God' claim against biblical adoption.
Defend adoption as a distinct grace of the gospel.
Synthesize adoption as the highest privilege of the justified.

BIB.11.9.6.t: Identify that God makes His people more holy.
Name the Holy Spirit as our helper to grow.
Recall that Christians turn away from sin.
Observe that growing in holiness takes a whole life.
Summarize sanctification (renewed in the whole person after God's image).
Explain dying to sin and living to righteousness.
Compare justification (declared once) with sanctification (renewed over time).
Apply the call to 'put off' the old self and 'put on' the new.
Interpret the Spirit-versus-flesh conflict in the believer.
Connect sanctification to union with Christ's death and resurrection.
Explain the means of grace in sanctification (Word, prayer, sacraments, fellowship).
Construct a theology of the mortification of sin.
Evaluate perfectionism and antinomianism as opposite errors.
Defend the necessity of holiness, without which none will see the Lord.
Synthesize sanctification as growth toward the image of Christ.

BIB.11.9.7.t: Identify that Jesus keeps His people safe forever.
Name Jesus as the Good Shepherd who never loses His sheep.
Recall that nothing can separate us from God's love.
Observe that God finishes the good work He begins.
Summarize the perseverance of the saints.
Explain that our security rests in God, not in ourselves.
Compare true perseverance with mere outward profession.
Apply the comfort of belonging to Christ in life and in death.
Analyze the ground of perseverance (election, Christ's intercession, the Spirit).
Interpret the warning passages within the doctrine of perseverance.
Connect perseverance to God's covenant faithfulness.
Explain assurance of salvation, its ground and its growth.
Construct a theology of assurance from 1 John.
Evaluate the loss-of-salvation view against the Reformed doctrine.
Defend perseverance without lapsing into presumption.
Synthesize perseverance and assurance as anchors for the Christian life.

BIB.11.9.8.t: Identify that believers will one day be perfect with Jesus.
Name heaven as being with the Lord forever.
Recall that our bodies will be raised.
Observe that we will be made like Jesus.
Explain the believer's union with Christ ('in Christ').
Compare our present adoption with our future glory.
Apply the hope of glory to present suffering.
Analyze union with Christ as the ground of every saving benefit.
Interpret the 'golden chain' ending in glorification.
Connect union with Christ to justification, sanctification, and glorification.
Explain the intermediate state and the final resurrection glory.
Construct a theology of glorification from Romans 8.
Evaluate views that collapse or deny bodily glorification.
Defend union with Christ as the very heart of salvation.
Synthesize the ordo salutis as one unbreakable work of grace, from election to glory.

BIB.1.1.1.t: Identify that God made the world because it is beautiful and ordered.
Name God as the First Maker (everything needs a maker).
Recall that the world didn't happen by accident.
Observe that a watch needs a watchmaker, and the world needs a Creator.
Summarize the idea of Cause and Effect (The Universe has a Cause).
Explain the Argument from Design (Complexity implies intelligence).
Compare a building (needs a builder) to the universe (needs a Creator).
Apply the Moral Argument: We know right and wrong because God exists.
Analyze the Kalam Cosmological Argument (Everything that begins to exist has a cause).
Connect the existence of objective moral values to a Moral Lawgiver.
Explain why an infinite regress of causes is impossible.
Construct a formal defense using the Ontological Argument (Anselm/Plantinga).
Evaluate Leibniz's Argument from Contingency (Why is there something rather than nothing?).
Defend theism against the 'God of the Gaps' objection.
Synthesize Classical arguments to build a cumulative case for theism.

BIB.1.1.2.t: Identify that the sky and trees tell us God is strong.
Name 'General Revelation' as God speaking through nature.
Recall that everyone knows there is a God (Romans 1).
Observe God's power in a storm or a mountain.
Summarize Psalm 19 ('The heavens declare the glory of God').
Explain that nature shows God exists, but not how to be saved.
Compare what we learn from a sunset vs. what we learn from the Bible.
Apply the truth that no one has an excuse for ignoring God.
Analyze the limits of Natural Theology (cannot reveal the Trinity or Atonement).
Interpret Romans 1:18-20 regarding the suppression of truth.
Connect the order of the universe to the mind of God (Logos).
Explain the relationship between Reason and Revelation.
Construct a historical overview of Natural Theology (Aquinas to Paley).
Evaluate the impact of Darwinism on the Argument from Design.
Defend the compatibility of Faith and Reason.
Produce an essay on the necessity of Special Revelation to complete General Revelation.

BIB.1.2.1.t: Identify that God made the world, it wasn't an accident.
Name 'Secular' as living like God isn't there.
Recall that we are made for a purpose.
Observe that people are sad without God.
Summarize what an Atheist believes (No God).
Explain that if there is no God, there is no real right or wrong.
Compare living for 'now' with living for eternity.
Apply the hope we have in Jesus.
Analyze the worldview of Materialism (only matter exists).
Interpret the logical end of Atheism (Nihilism/Meaninglessness).
Connect Darwinian evolution to the devaluation of human life.
Construct a critique of Secular Humanism.
Evaluate the problem of evil for the Atheist (no standard of 'good').
Defend the necessity of God for meaning, value, and purpose.
Synthesize the Christian worldview as the only one that fits reality.

BIB.1.2.2.t: Identify that not everyone who says 'Jesus' believes the Bible.
Name the Bible as our only special book.
Recall that Jesus is God, not an angel or a brother of Satan.
Observe that we must be careful who we listen to.
Summarize the main error of JWs (Jesus is not God).
Explain the main error of Mormons (Adding books to the Bible).
Compare the Trinity with the false views of cults.
Apply the warning to not add or subtract from Scripture.
Analyze the history of Joseph Smith and Charles Taze Russell.
Interpret the translation errors in the New World Translation (John 1:1).
Connect the cults' demand for works to the denial of grace.
Explain how to share the true Gospel with a cult member.
Construct a theological refutation of Arianism (JWs) and Polytheism (LDS).
Evaluate the psychological structure of cult control.
Defend the biblical definition of the Trinity and Hypostatic Union.
Produce a comparison chart of key doctrines: God, Jesus, Salvation, Scripture.

BIB.1.2.3.t: Identify that God is a Person, not a 'force' or 'energy'.
Name magic and horoscopes as things God hates.
Recall that we pray to God, not crystals or stars.
Observe that Jesus is the only Light.
Summarize the idea of Pantheism (God is everything).
Explain why we don't play with Ouija boards or spirits.
Compare the Creator/Creature distinction with the idea that 'we are all gods'.
Apply the command to have no other gods before Him.
Analyze the worldview of Monism (All is One).
Interpret the danger of 'Christ Consciousness' vs. the Person of Christ.
Connect Gnosticism (secret knowledge) to New Age thought.
Explain the spiritual danger of the occult (Deuteronomy 18).
Construct a critique of Moral Relativism in New Age spirituality.
Evaluate the influence of Eastern Mysticism on Western culture (Yoga/Meditation roots).
Defend the distinct personality of God against Pantheism.
Synthesize the biblical view of spiritual warfare regarding the occult.

BIB.1.2.4.t: Identify that we are saved by faith, not by doing chores.
Name Jesus as the one we pray to, not Mary or saints.
Recall that the Bible is our boss, not the Pope.
Observe that we love our Catholic neighbors but disagree on how we are saved.
Summarize the 'Five Solas' of the Reformation.
Explain the difference between Grace Alone and Grace + Works.
Compare the Priest in the OT with Jesus our High Priest.
Apply the truth that Scripture is enough (Sola Scriptura).
Analyze the issue of Authority (Scripture vs. Tradition + Magisterium).
Interpret the Roman view of Justification (process) vs. Biblical (declaration).
Connect the Mass/Eucharist to the finished work of Christ.
Explain the error of Purgatory and Indulgences.
Construct a historical overview of the Council of Trent.
Evaluate the doctrine of Papal Infallibility.
Defend the doctrine of Imputation vs. Infusion of righteousness.
Produce an essay on the Mariology dogmas (Immaculate Conception, Assumption).

BIB.1.3.1.t: Name the eyewitnesses (Mary, Peter, the disciples).
Recall that Jesus ate food after He came back to life.
Observe that the disciples were not afraid anymore.
Summarize the events of Easter morning.
Explain why the disciples wouldn't die for a lie.
Compare the Swoon Theory (he fainted) with what really happened.
Apply the fact of the Resurrection to our own hope.
Interpret the conversion of skeptics like James and Paul.
Connect the rise of the early church to the reality of the Resurrection.
Explain why the 'Stolen Body' theory fails.
Construct a legal/historical defense of the Resurrection.
Defend the bodily nature of the resurrection against spiritualized interpretations.
Produce an essay on the Trilemma (Liar, Lunatic, or Lord).

BIB.1.3.2.t: Identify a miracle as something wonderful only God can do.
Name Jesus' power over storms and sickness.
Recall that miracles showed Jesus was God's Son.
Observe that magic tricks are not miracles.
Summarize why Jesus performed miracles (compassion and proof).
Explain the difference between magic and a miracle.
Compare the miracles of Jesus with the 'miracles' of other religions.
Analyze the definition of a miracle (divine intervention in natural law).
Interpret Nicodemus' statement: 'No one can do these signs unless God is with him.'
Connect the cessation/continuation debate to apologetics (do miracles happen today?).
Explain the 'Sign' theology in John's Gospel.
Construct a refutation of David Hume's argument against miracles.
Evaluate the claim that science disproves miracles.
Defend the Resurrection as the 'Grand Miracle' that validates all others.
Produce a reflection on the relationship between faith and evidence.

BIB.1.3.3.t: Identify that God knows the future.
Name Bethlehem as the place God promised Jesus would be born.
Recall that Jesus did everything God promised.
Observe that only God can tell what will happen 100% of the time.
Summarize the prophecies of the Crucifixion (Psalm 22, Isaiah 53).
Explain how Jesus fulfilled the Passover.
Compare vague predictions (horoscopes) with specific Bible prophecies.
Apply the certainty of future promises based on past fulfillment.
Analyze the statistical probability of one man fulfilling all messianic prophecies.
Interpret Daniel's prophecy of the empires.
Connect the destruction of Tyre (Ezekiel) to historical fulfillment.
Construct a list of major Messianic prophecies and their NT citations.
Evaluate the objection that Jesus 'maneuvered' to fulfill prophecy.
Defend the supernatural origin of the Bible based on predictive prophecy.
Synthesize the argument from prophecy with the argument from miracles.

BIB.1.3.4.t: Identify the Bible as a true book, not a fairy tale.
Name the Scribes as men who copied the Bible carefully.
Recall that the stories in the Bible really happened.
Observe that we have many, many old copies of the Bible.
Summarize how we know the Bible hasn't been changed (Manuscripts).
Explain that archaeology finds things that match Bible stories.
Compare the number of Bible copies with other old books.
Apply confidence in the Bible when others say it is made up.
Analyze the 'Telephone Game' objection and why it doesn't apply to Scripture.
Interpret the significance of the Dead Sea Scrolls.
Connect the short time gap between events and writing to historical accuracy.
Explain the difference between a translation and a transmission error.
Construct a defense of the text based on Bibliographical, Internal, and External tests.
Evaluate Bart Ehrman's critique of textual variants.
Defend the reliability of the New Testament against the 'Da Vinci Code' style conspiracies.
Synthesize the history of the English Bible and manuscript families.

BIB.1.4.1.t: Identify when someone says something that doesn't make sense.
Recall that we should answer foolishness wisely.
Observe that people who don't know God are confused.
Summarize how to ask 'How do you know that?'
Explain that non-Christians have to 'borrow' Christian ideas (like right and wrong).
Compare a house built on sand (unbelief) vs. rock (Christ).
Apply Proverbs 26:4-5 (Answer a fool according to his folly).
Analyze a worldview to see if it contradicts itself (e.g., 'There is no absolute truth').
Connect the lack of a moral standard in atheism to the problem of evil.
Explain how to expose the arbitrariness of non-Christian claims.
Construct an internal critique of Materialism (it destroys reason/free will).
Defend the faith by showing that non-Christian systems collapse on their own terms.
Synthesize the 'reductio ad absurdum' method in apologetics.

BIB.1.4.2.t: Identify that numbers and logic come from God.
Name God as the one who makes things make sense.
Recall that if there was no God, we couldn't know anything for sure.
Observe that even people who don't love God use God's logic.
Summarize why we can trust our minds (because God made them).
Explain that laws of logic (like math) don't change.
Compare a random universe (chaos) with God's universe (order).
Apply the idea that atheists are borrowing from God's world to argue against Him.
Analyze the preconditions of intelligibility (Logic, Morality, Uniformity of Nature).
Interpret the 'Problem of Induction' (why will the sun rise tomorrow?).
Connect the laws of logic to the nature of God (universal, invariant, abstract).
Explain why materialism cannot account for the laws of logic.
Construct the Transcendental Argument for God (TAG).
Defend the Christian worldview as the only basis for rational thought.
Produce an essay on Van Til's apologetic method.

BIB.1.4.3.t: Name God's Word as the boss of truth.
Recall that wearing different glasses makes the world look different.
Observe that some people don't believe the Bible.
Summarize what a 'Worldview' is (how we see everything).
Explain that everyone has faith in something (God or themselves).
Compare the Christian view (God made us) with the Secular view (we are accidents).
Apply the Bible as the starting point for thinking.
Analyze the concept of a 'Presupposition' (an assumption taken for granted).
Interpret the myth of neutrality (no one is neutral).
Connect the fear of the Lord to the beginning of knowledge.
Explain why evidence alone doesn't convince everyone (Romans 1).
Construct a diagram of the 'Archimedean Point' (Ultimate Authority).
Evaluate why Empiricism and Rationalism fail as ultimate standards.
Defend the necessity of the Christian worldview to make sense of anything.
Synthesize the relationship between circular reasoning and ultimate authorities.

BIB.2.1.1.t: Identify that God made the world good.
Name the sad day when Adam and Eve disobeyed.
Recall that Jesus came to rescue us.
Observe that one day God will make everything new.
Summarize the four main parts of the Bible's big story.
Explain why we need a Rescuer (because of the Fall).
Compare the Garden of Eden with the New Jerusalem.
Apply the hope of Restoration to a bad day.
Analyze how individual Bible stories fit into the larger arc.
Interpret the 'Proto-evangelium' (Gen 3:15) as the first promise of Redemption.
Connect the Fall to the brokenness seen in the world today.
Explain the consistency of God's plan from Genesis to Revelation.
Construct a diagram of the meta-narrative timeline.
Evaluate other worldviews against the linear history of Scripture.
Defend the necessity of a historical Fall for the logic of the Gospel.
Synthesize the believer's role in the current 'Redemption' phase.

BIB.2.1.2.t: Identify a promise as something special you keep.
Name the rainbow as God's promise to Noah.
Recall that God promised Abraham a big family.
Observe that God never breaks a promise.
Summarize God's promise to David (a King forever).
Explain the difference between a rule (Law) and a promise (Covenant).
Compare the Old Covenant (Stone tablets) with the New Covenant (Heart).
Identify the signs of the covenants (Rainbow, Circumcision, Sabbath, Cup).
Analyze the conditional vs. unconditional nature of specific covenants.
Connect the Abrahamic promise to the coming of Christ.
Explain how the Mosaic covenant showed our sin.
Construct a chart tracing the progressive revelation of the covenants.
Defend the unity of the Covenant of Grace across the ages.
Synthesize Christ as the mediator and fulfillment of all covenants.

BIB.2.1.3.t: Identify a picture that looks like something real.
Recall that Noah's Ark saved people, just like Jesus saves us.
Observe that the Old Testament points to Jesus.
Summarize how the Tabernacle teaches us about God's holiness.
Explain what a 'Shadow' is in the Bible (Colossians 2).
Compare the Bronze Serpent with Jesus on the Cross (John 3).
Identify Joseph as a type of Christ (suffering servant/ruler).
Analyze the criteria for a valid biblical type.
Interpret the priesthood of Aaron as a type of Christ's priesthood.
Connect the Manna in the wilderness to the Bread of Life.
Explain the typology of the Temple.
Construct a study of the Day of Atonement typology.
Evaluate the danger of allegorizing vs. reading typologically.
Defend the Christocentric reading of the Old Testament.
Synthesize the 'Greater than' pattern (Jesus is the greater Moses/David/Solomon).

BIB.2.1.4.t: Recall that Jesus is ruling right now.
Observe that there is still sadness in the world.
Summarize the parables of the Kingdom (Mustard Seed, Treasure).
Explain that Jesus defeated sin, but we still fight it.
Compare the Kingdom of the World with the Kingdom of God.
Analyze the 'Inaugurated Eschatology' (The Kingdom is here).
Interpret the miracles as breaking-in of the Kingdom.
Connect the Resurrection to the start of the New Creation.
Explain the tension of living between the times.
Construct a theology of Christian engagement in culture.
Evaluate the error of over-realized eschatology (expecting perfection now).
Defend the spiritual nature of the Kingdom vs. political expectations.
Synthesize the hope of the final consummation with present faithfulness.

BIB.2.2.1.t: Identify Matthew, Mark, and Luke as three books that tell similar stories.
Name John as the fourth story about Jesus.
Recall that they all tell the truth about Jesus.
Observe that John talks a lot about 'Love' and 'Light'.
Summarize why the first three are called 'Synoptic' (seen together).
Explain that John focuses on who Jesus is (God).
Compare a story in Mark with the same story in Luke.
Identify the 'I AM' statements in John.
Analyze the literary relationship between Matthew, Mark, and Luke.
Interpret the Prologue of John (The Word was God).
Connect the distinct audiences (Jews vs. Gentiles) to the gospel variations.
Explain the priority of Mark (common theory).
Construct a harmony of a specific event (e.g., the Feeding of the 5000) across all four.
Evaluate the unique theological contribution of John's Gospel.
Defend the reliability of having four distinct witnesses.
Synthesize the four-fold portrait of Christ (King, Servant, Man, God).

BIB.2.2.2.t: Identify the Holy Spirit coming like fire.
Name Peter and Paul as leaders.
Recall that the church started in Jerusalem.
Observe that the believers shared everything.
Summarize the spread of the Gospel (Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria, Ends of the Earth).
Compare the boldness of Peter after Pentecost with his fear before.
Identify the conversion of Saul to Paul.
Analyze the conflict and resolution in Acts 15 (Jerusalem Council).
Interpret the significance of the inclusion of Gentiles (Cornelius).
Connect the missionary journeys to the geography of Rome.
Explain the role of persecution in spreading the church.
Construct a timeline of the major events in Acts.
Evaluate the prescriptive vs. descriptive nature of events in Acts.
Defend the work of the Holy Spirit as the primary actor in Acts.
Synthesize the transition from a Jewish sect to a global faith.

BIB.2.2.3.t: Identify a letter in the Bible.
Name Paul as a man who wrote many letters.
Recall that letters were sent to churches.
Observe greetings at the start of books like Romans.
Summarize the typical parts of a letter (Greeting, Body, Farewell).
Explain why Paul wrote letters (to teach and correct).
Compare a personal letter (Philemon) with a church letter (Ephesians).
Identify the scribe or co-sender (e.g., Timothy).
Analyze the 'Occasional' nature of the epistles (written for specific problems).
Interpret the cultural background of specific commands (e.g., head coverings).
Connect the doctrine (Indicative) to the duty (Imperative).
Explain the role of the amanuensis (secretary).
Construct a background profile for the city of Corinth.
Evaluate the principle of universality (why these letters apply to us).
Defend the authority of the Apostles' letters as Scripture.
Synthesize the theology of Paul across multiple epistles.

BIB.2.2.4.t: Name John as the man who saw the vision.
Recall that Jesus wins in the end.
Observe strange creatures and dragons in the story.
Summarize the promise that God will wipe away every tear.
Explain that 'Apocalypse' means revealing or uncovering.
Compare the scary beasts with the Lion of Judah.
Identify heaven as a place with no more pain.
Analyze the use of numbers and symbols (7, 12, 666).
Interpret the purpose of the book (to encourage suffering Christians).
Connect the imagery of Revelation to Daniel and Ezekiel.
Explain the four main approaches to interpretation (Preterist, Historicist, Futurist, Idealist).
Construct a study of the Throne Room vision (Rev 4-5).
Evaluate the danger of date-setting and speculation.
Defend the sovereignty of God over history.
Synthesize the worship of the Lamb as the climax of history.

BIB.2.3.1.t: Identify the first five books of the Bible.
Name Moses as the main writer.
Observe the story of Creation and the Exodus.
Explain the importance of the Tabernacle.
Compare the narratives (Genesis) with the laws (Leviticus).
Analyze the structure of the Suzerain-Vassal treaty in Deuteronomy.
Interpret the holiness code and its fulfillment.
Connect the Patriarchal promises to the Nation of Israel.
Construct a timeline of the Pentateuch.
Evaluate the Documentary Hypothesis (JEDP) from a conservative viewpoint.
Defend the Mosaic authorship and historicity.
Synthesize the foundational theology of God, Man, and Covenant.
Name Jesus as the Lamb of God.

BIB.2.3.2.t: Recall that Israel wanted a king.
Observe that obeying God brings blessing, disobeying brings trouble.
Summarize the cycle of the Judges.
Explain why the kingdom split (Solomon's sin/Rehoboam's pride).
Compare good kings (Hezekiah) with bad kings (Ahab).
Interpret the role of the Prophet in checking the King.
Connect the Land to the Covenant.
Explain the decline from Conquest to Exile.
Construct a synchronized timeline of the Divided Monarchy.
Evaluate the character of David as a 'man after God's own heart'.
Defend the justice of God in the Exile.
Synthesize the theme of God's faithfulness despite human failure.

BIB.2.3.3.t: Name Solomon as the wise man (Proverbs).
Recall that 'The Lord is my Shepherd'.
Observe poetry and feelings in these books.
Summarize the fear of the Lord as the beginning of wisdom.
Explain the difference between a Proverb (general truth) and a Promise.
Compare the suffering of Job with the confidence of Psalms.
Interpret the problem of evil in Job.
Connect the Psalms to the prayer life of Jesus.
Construct a classification of Psalms (Lament, Praise, Royal).
Evaluate the theology of suffering in Wisdom literature.
Defend the practical value of Proverbs for daily living.
Synthesize the pursuit of wisdom as the pursuit of Christ.

BIB.2.3.4.t: Identify a prophet as God's messenger.
Recall that they warned people to stop sinning.
Observe promises about a coming Savior.
Summarize the message: Repent or Judgment will come.
Explain the difference between Major (long) and Minor (short) books.
Compare Jonah (ran away) with Isaiah (said 'Send me').
Identify Daniel in the lions' den.
Analyze the 'Day of the Lord' theme.
Interpret the New Covenant prophecy in Jeremiah 31.
Connect the Suffering Servant (Isaiah 53) to Jesus.
Explain the function of the prophet as a covenant lawyer.
Construct a timeline placing prophets with the kings they served.
Evaluate the imagery of spiritual adultery in Hosea.
Defend the predictive nature of prophecy.
Synthesize the dual message of judgment and restoration.

BIB.2.4.1.t: Identify the Bible as God's special book that should be opened every day.
Observe a parent or teacher reading the Bible and imitate the posture of listening.
Name specific times of the day (morning or night) when we can hear from God.
Ask to hear stories from the Bible as part of a daily routine.
Explain why reading the Bible daily is food for the Christian soul.
Apply a simple checklist to track reading the Bible for a full week.
Compare the habit of Bible reading to other daily habits like brushing teeth or eating.
Summarize the main thought of a short daily passage in a journal.
Analyze personal schedules to identify obstacles to consistent Bible reading.
Connect the practice of daily reading to the concept of 'abiding' in Christ (John 15).
