Explain the difference between reading for information and reading for transformation.
Evaluate different times of day to determine when personal focus is highest for reading.
Construct a sustainable, long-term plan for reading through the entire Bible.
Evaluate the spiritual impact of inconsistency and develop strategies for discipline.
Defend the necessity of daily Scripture intake against the cultural pressure of busyness.
Synthesize daily reading habits with deep study to produce a holistic view of Scripture.

BIB.2.4.2.t: Observe what is happening in a picture of a Bible story.
Ask 'Who?', 'What?', and 'Where?' questions about a story.
Identify the main person in the story.
Retell what happened in the beginning, middle, and end.
Summarize the three steps: Observation, Interpretation, Application.
Apply specific color codes to mark key words in a printed text.
Explain why we must look at what the text says before what it means.
Compare the characters in a story to understand their choices.
Analyze a paragraph by circling key words, listing facts, and noting contrasts.
Interpret the meaning of a passage based only on the observations made.
Connect the interpretation to a specific, actionable application.
Explain the danger of jumping to application without proper observation.
Construct a full inductive study of a New Testament epistle (Observation, Interpretation, Application).
Evaluate different commentaries to check personal interpretation.
Perform independent research on historical background to aid observation.
Produce a teaching outline based on the inductive study of a passage.

BIB.2.4.3.t: Memorize short key verses (e.g., Genesis 1:1, John 3:16).
Repeat a verse out loud until it can be said without help.
Identify a verse that brings comfort when afraid.
Copy a memory verse in best handwriting.
Memorize longer passages or sets of verses (e.g., The Beatitudes, Psalm 23).
Explain the meaning of a memorized verse in own words.
Apply a memorized verse to a specific temptation or struggle.
Compare the difference between just knowing the words and thinking about them (meditation).
Analyze a memorized passage by breaking it down phrase by phrase.
Connect memorized verses to other parts of the Bible to support a doctrine.
Explain the Puritan concept of 'chewing' on the Word (meditation) for spiritual nourishment.
Research the context of a memory verse to ensure it is applied correctly.
Construct a system for retaining and reviewing memorized Scripture over time.
Evaluate the role of meditation in fighting sin and cultivating joy.
Produce a written meditation on a passage, exploring its implications deeply.
Defend the discipline of 'hiding God's Word in the heart' as essential for spiritual warfare.

BIB.2.4.4.t: Identify what a Bible story teaches us about God's love.
Ask, 'What does God want me to do?' after hearing a story.
Copy a short verse that helps us trust Jesus.
Express thanks to God for the truth found in His Word.
Apply a specific command from Scripture to a situation at school or home.
Explain how a passage encourages us to love God or love our neighbor.
Summarize what a text reveals about God's character (e.g., He is holy, He is kind).
Participate in a guided prayer based on a Psalm.
Analyze own heart responses to Scripture (conviction, comfort, or confusion).
Connect the truths of a passage to personal struggles and doubts.
Explain how the Holy Spirit uses the Word to change our hearts.
Interpret the difference between moralism (being good) and gospel fruit (loving Christ).
Evaluate personal life choices in light of specific Scriptural principles.
Construct prayers that are saturated with the language and theology of the text read.
Produce a devotional reflection that applies deep theological truth to daily life.
Defend the practice of reading for relationship over reading for mere academic knowledge.

BIB.2.4.5.t: Retell the main events of a Bible story in the correct order.
Identify the main character in a Bible story.
Ask questions about words or ideas in the Bible that are hard to understand.
Describe what happens in a story using pictures or simple words.
Summarize the 'Who, What, When, Where' of a passage.
Explain the plain meaning of a text without adding to it.
Categorize a passage as a story, a song, or a rule/command.
Compare two different stories to find similarities in how God acts.
Analyze a passage to determine the author's main point.
Interpret the meaning of key words within their immediate context.
Explain the difference between observation (what it says) and interpretation (what it means).
Connect a specific passage to the broader context of the chapter.
Evaluate a text to determine the author's logical flow and argument.
Construct a detailed outline of a biblical chapter or book.
Perform independent word studies to clarify the meaning of crucial terms.
Produce a written summary of a passage that accurately reflects the author's intent.

BIB.2.4.6.t: Listen quietly to a short Bible reading.
Identify one word or phrase that stands out.
Ask God to help understand the special word.
Express a simple prayer back to God about the reading.
Summarize the four steps: Read, Think, Pray, Rest (Lectio, Meditatio, Oratio, Contemplatio).
Apply the method to a short Psalm.
Explain what it feels like to listen to God through His Word.
Participate in a guided time of quiet reading and prayer.
Analyze how slowing down reading helps notice details often missed.
Interpret the difference between studying for facts and reading for communion.
Connect the historical practice of Lectio Divina to the modern quiet time.
Explain how 'chewing' on the text (Meditatio) leads to prayer (Oratio).
Evaluate the benefits of contemplative reading in a distracted digital age.
Construct a personal rhythm of reading that incorporates silence and reflection.
Produce a journal entry documenting the movement from reading to contemplation.
Defend the historical validity of this practice within the Protestant tradition.

BIB.2.4.7.t: Recall that the Bible has two main parts: the Old Testament and the New Testament.
Identify the very first book (Genesis) and the very last book (Revelation).
Follow along in a picture Bible as an adult reads through major stories.
Name the four Gospels as the stories about Jesus.
Categorize Bible books into Law, History, Poetry, Prophecy, Gospels, and Letters.
Summarize the general flow of the Bible from Creation to the New Heavens.
Apply a reading plan to finish one entire book of the Bible.
Compare the length and style of different books (e.g., Psalms vs. Mark).
Analyze the structure of a canonical reading plan versus a chronological one.
Connect individual books to the larger metanarrative of Scripture.
Explain the value of reading the 'whole counsel of God' rather than just favorite verses.
Interpret how the Old Testament prepares the way for the New Testament.
Evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of different reading plans (M’Cheyne, Chronological, etc.).
Construct a personalized plan to read the entire Bible in one or two years.
Perform independent research to understand the historical setting of the books being read.
Produce a synthesis of a major theme traced through a whole-Bible reading.

BIB.3.1.10.t: Identify Saul as the first king and David as the best king.
Retell the story of David and Goliath.
Name Solomon as the king who built God's house (Temple).
Recall that David wrote songs to God (Psalms).
Summarize how David was chosen (heart vs. outward appearance).
Explain why Saul lost the kingdom.
Compare David's repentance (Psalm 51) with Saul's excuses.
Apply lessons from Solomon's wisdom and his foolishness (many wives).
Interpret the political and spiritual consolidation of Jerusalem.
Connect Solomon's Temple dedication prayer to God's global purpose.
Explain the consequences of David's sin with Bathsheba on his family.
Construct a profile of the 'Messianic King' based on the United Monarchy.
Evaluate the tension between the theocracy and the monarchy.
Perform research on the historical wealth and trade of Solomon's kingdom.
Synthesize the rise and peak of Israel's history as a type of the Kingdom of God.

BIB.3.1.1.t: Identify Joshua as the new leader after Moses.
Retell the story of the walls of Jericho falling down.
Name Rahab as the woman who helped the spies.
Recall that the people promised to serve the Lord.
Summarize the crossing of the Jordan River on dry ground.
Explain why Achan's sin caused the whole nation to lose a battle.
Compare the spies who trusted God (Joshua/Caleb) with those who didn't.
Apply the phrase 'As for me and my house, we will serve the Lord.'
Analyze the military strategy and divine intervention in the conquest campaigns.
Interpret the ethical difficulty of the Canaanite conquest (God's judgment on sin).
Connect the allotment of the land to God fulfilling His promise to Abraham.
Explain the significance of the Cities of Refuge.
Construct a theological defense of Holy War in the OT context.
Evaluate the incompleteness of the conquest and its future consequences.
Perform research on the archaeological evidence for the conquest of Jericho/Ai.
Synthesize the theme of 'Rest' in Joshua with Hebrews 4.

BIB.3.1.2.t: Identify God as the maker of the world and the first family (Adam and Eve).
Retell the story of Noah and the Ark using pictures or toys.
Name Cain and Abel as the first brothers.
Recall that sin made the world a sad and hard place.
Summarize the sequence of events: Creation, Fall, Cain/Abel, Flood, Babel.
Explain why God sent the Flood (judgment on wickedness).
Compare the world before the Flood with the world after.
Categorize the sons of Noah (Shem, Ham, Japheth) as the fathers of nations.
Analyze the downward spiral of sin from the Garden to Babel.
Interpret the 'Table of Nations' in Genesis 10 as the origin of diverse cultures.
Connect the Tower of Babel judgment to the Great Commission (reversing the confusion).
Explain the significance of the 'Proto-evangelium' (Gen 3:15) in the early narrative.
Construct a timeline of Primeval History using biblical genealogies.
Evaluate different interpretations of the 'Sons of God' in Genesis 6.
Defend the historicity of Adam and the Flood against mythical interpretations.
Synthesize the theology of creation and judgment found in Genesis 1-11.

BIB.3.1.3.t: Identify Elijah as the prophet who called down fire.
Name Jonah as the prophet who was swallowed by a big fish.
Recall that the kingdom split into two parts: North and South.
Observe that bad kings led people away from God.
Summarize the contest on Mount Carmel with the prophets of Baal.
Explain why the kingdom divided (Rehoboam's foolishness).
Compare the Northern Kingdom (Israel) and the Southern Kingdom (Judah).
Categorize prophets by who they spoke to (Israel, Judah, or other nations).
Analyze the sin of Jeroboam (golden calves) and its lasting effect.
Interpret the role of the prophet as a covenant lawyer prosecuting the nation.
Connect the fall of Samaria (722 BC) to the Assyrian empire.
Explain the reforms of Hezekiah and Josiah.
Construct a timeline of the kings and the prophets who ministered to them.
Evaluate the geopolitical situation involving Assyria, Babylon, and Egypt.
Defend the justice of the Exile based on the warnings of Deuteronomy.
Produce a study on the 'Day of the Lord' theme in the prophets.

BIB.3.1.4.t: Identify the Holy Spirit as the helper Jesus sent.
Name Peter and Paul as men who told the world about Jesus.
Recall that the first church shared their food and money.
Observe how the church grew from a few people to many.
Summarize the story of Pentecost and the tongues of fire.
Compare the church in Jerusalem with the missionary journeys of Paul.
Apply the boldness of the apostles to sharing faith today.
Analyze the conflict regarding Gentiles and the Law (Acts 15).
Interpret the significance of the destruction of the Temple in AD 70.
Connect the missionary journeys to the geography of the Roman Empire.
Explain the role of persecution in spreading the Gospel.
Construct a map of the spread of Christianity in the first century.
Evaluate the transition from Jewish sect to global religion.
Perform research on the martyrdom of the Apostles.
Synthesize the main themes of the Apostolic preaching (Kerygma).

BIB.3.1.5.t: Identify Daniel in the lions' den.
Name Queen Esther who saved her people.
Recall that the people came back to build the walls of Jerusalem.
Observe that God was with them even when they were far from home.
Summarize the story of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego.
Compare the rebuilding of the Temple (Ezra) with the rebuilding of the Wall (Nehemiah).
Apply Nehemiah's prayer and hard work to a personal task.
Analyze the providence of God in the book of Esther (where God is not named).
Interpret the vision of the Valley of Dry Bones in Ezekiel.
Connect the decree of Cyrus to the prophecy of Jeremiah (70 years).
Explain the problem of the people's hearts remaining hard even after the return.
Construct a historical overview of the Persian Empire's role in biblical history.
Evaluate the spiritual condition of the post-exilic community through Malachi.
Defend the faithfulness of God in preserving the Davidic line during the Exile.
Synthesize the 'already/not yet' nature of the restoration in the OT.

BIB.3.1.6.t: Identify Moses as the baby in the basket who became a leader.
Name the Red Sea crossing as God's great rescue.
Recall the Ten Commandments as God's good rules.
Observe how God fed the people with manna in the desert.
Summarize the ten plagues and why God sent them (to show He is the true God).
Explain the meaning of the Passover meal.
Compare the Golden Calf incident with true worship.
Categorize the furniture in the Tabernacle (Ark, Table, Lampstand).
Analyze the hardening of Pharaoh's heart.
Interpret the symbolism of the Tabernacle and the High Priest's garments.
Connect the rebellion at Kadesh Barnea to the 40 years of wandering.
Explain the Holiness Code in Leviticus (God dwelling among His people).
Construct a map of the likely route of the Exodus.
Evaluate the date of the Exodus (Early vs. Late date theories).
Defend the Mosaic Law as a reflection of God's character, not arbitrary rules.
Produce an essay on the Typology of the Exodus as a pattern for salvation.

BIB.3.1.7.t: Identify Samson as the strong man and Gideon as the brave leader.
Name the Judges as helpers God sent when the people were in trouble.
Recall that the people kept forgetting God.
Observe that God always forgave them when they prayed.
Summarize the cycle of Judges: Sin, Slavery, Supplication, Salvation.
Explain why Gideon used only 300 men.
Compare Deborah (a good judge) with Samson (a flawed judge).
Categorize the enemies of Israel (Philistines, Midianites, Moabites).
Analyze the refrain 'In those days there was no king in Israel.'
Interpret the story of Jephthah's vow.
Connect the moral decline in Judges to the need for a righteous King.
Explain the role of the 'Kinsman-Redeemer' in the book of Ruth (set during Judges).
Construct a chart tracking the spiraling depravity from Othniel to Samson.
Evaluate the role of women in the book of Judges.
Defend the sovereignty of God in using flawed leaders.
Produce a thematic study on 'Apostasy' using the book of Judges.

BIB.3.1.8.t: Identify the manger, the cross, and the empty tomb.
Name the disciples who followed Jesus.
Retell a parable like the Lost Sheep or Good Samaritan.
Express that Jesus is God who became a man.
Summarize the baptism and temptation of Jesus.
Explain the meaning of the 'Incarnation' (God putting on flesh).
Categorize Jesus' ministry into teaching, healing, and suffering.
Compare the responses of the Pharisees vs. the sinners to Jesus.
Analyze the 'I Am' statements in the Gospel of John.
Interpret the Sermon on the Mount as the ethic of the Kingdom.
Connect the Transfiguration to the glory of God in the OT.
Explain the significance of the Ascension for the church today.
Construct a harmony of the Gospels for the Passion Week.
Evaluate the hypostatic union (fully God, fully man) and why it matters.
Defend the miracles of Jesus against naturalistic skepticism.
Produce an essay on how Jesus fulfills the three offices: Prophet, Priest, King.

BIB.3.1.9.t: Identify Abraham as the man who believed God's promise.
Name Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph as the fathers of Israel.
Retell the story of Joseph's coat and his journey to Egypt.
Recall that God changed Jacob's name to Israel.
Summarize the call of Abraham and his journey to Canaan.
Explain how Jacob tricked Esau but later learned to trust God.
Compare the faith of Abraham with the mistakes he made (like lying about Sarah).
Trace the movement of God's people from Ur to Canaan to Egypt.
Analyze the testing of Abraham's faith in Genesis 22 (The Binding of Isaac).
Interpret Joseph's statement: 'You meant it for evil, but God meant it for good.'
Connect the twelve sons of Jacob to the Twelve Tribes of Israel.
Explain the concept of Election through the choice of Isaac over Ishmael, and Jacob over Esau.
Construct a family tree of the Patriarchs including wives and key descendants.
Evaluate the cultural context of patriarchal customs (covenants, birthrights, marriage).
Defend the providence of God in preserving the messianic line through famine and conflict.
Synthesize the Abrahamic Covenant with the rest of redemptive history.

BIB.3.2.1.t: Observe that blood was used in the Bible for forgiveness.
Summarize the story of Abraham and Isaac (God provides the ram).
Compare the Passover lamb with Jesus.
Analyze the necessity of substitution (someone taking our place).
Interpret the tearing of the Temple curtain.
Construct a study on the phrase 'Behold the Lamb'.
Evaluate the inadequacy of animal sacrifices.
Defend the Penal Substitutionary nature of the Atonement.
Synthesize the theme of blood sacrifice from Eden to Heaven.

BIB.3.2.2.t: Identify the Temple as God's house.
Name the Garden of Eden as the first place God walked with man.
Recall that God wants to be with us.
Observe that the Temple was beautiful and holy.
Summarize God's presence in the Tabernacle (cloud/fire).
Explain why we are now the Temple (Holy Spirit in us).
Compare Solomon's Temple with the New Jerusalem (no temple needed).
Analyze the separation between God and man caused by sin.
Interpret Ezekiel's vision of the glory leaving and returning.
Connect Jesus as the true Temple (destroy this temple and I will raise it).
Construct a theology of the Presence of God.
Evaluate the significance of the church as a spiritual house.
Defend the holiness required to dwell with God.
Synthesize the trajectory from Eden to the New Earth.

BIB.3.2.3.t: Name a priest as someone who prays for us.
Recall that a prophet speaks God's words.
Observe that Jesus does all three jobs.
Explain how Jesus is a Prophet (He teaches).
Compare David (King) and Moses (Prophet) with Jesus.
Identify 'Christ' as the Greek word for Messiah.
Analyze the anointing of leaders in the OT.
Explain the Kingship of Christ over the nations.
Construct a profile of the Munus Triplex (Threefold Office).
Evaluate how the church participates in these offices.
Defend Jesus as the final Word, final Sacrifice, and final Authority.
Synthesize the fulfillment of all OT offices in Christ.

BIB.3.2.4.t: Identify that God always has friends.
Name Noah's family (the ones who were saved).
Recall that not everyone listens to God.
Observe that God keeps His people safe.
Summarize the story of Elijah (7,000 who did not bow to Baal).
Explain what 'Remnant' means (a small piece left over).
Compare the crowd with the disciples.
Analyze the concept of the faithful minority.
Interpret the olive tree metaphor in Romans 11.
Connect the Remnant to the doctrine of Election.
Explain the invisible church vs. visible church.
Construct a history of the Remnant through the Bible.
Evaluate the preservation of the church through history.
Defend the faithfulness of God to His promises despite apostasy.
Synthesize the continuity of the People of God (Israel and the Church).

BIB.4.1.1.t: Identify a heresy as a lie about God.
Name the truth: Jesus is God and Man.
Recall that we must be careful what we listen to.
Observe that the Bible helps us spot lies.
Summarize the error of Gnosticism (Body is bad, Spirit is good).
Explain why Arianism (Jesus is a creature) is wrong.
Compare truth with a counterfeit (looks real but isn't).
Apply the need to know the real Jesus.
Analyze the danger of Marcionism (rejecting the Old Testament).
Interpret the error of Pelagianism (we can save ourselves).
Connect ancient heresies to modern cults (e.g., Arianism -> Jehovah's Witnesses).
Construct a taxonomy of Christological heresies.
Evaluate the church's response to heresy (it sharpened doctrine).
Defend the biblical view of sin against Pelagius.

BIB.4.1.2.t: Identify that early Christians were hurt for loving Jesus.
Name the Catacombs as places where they hid and prayed.
Recall that Jesus said the world would hate His friends.
Observe that the church grew even when it was hard.
Summarize the persecution under Nero (fire in Rome).
Explain why Romans thought Christians were 'haters of mankind'.
Compare the safety we have today with the danger back then.
Apply the courage of Perpetua and Felicity.
Analyze the saying 'The blood of the martyrs is the seed of the church'.
Interpret the political reasons for persecution (refusing to say 'Caesar is Lord').
Connect the suffering of the church to the suffering of Christ.
Explain the Decian and Diocletian persecutions.
Evaluate the legal status of Christianity (Religio Illicita) in the Roman Empire.
Defend the witness of the martyrs as an apologetic for the truth.
Produce a reflection on the cost of discipleship then and now.

BIB.4.1.3.t: Identify monks as men who lived alone to pray.
Name Anthony as a man who went to the desert.
Recall that they wanted to be close to God.
Observe that they gave up their money and houses.
Summarize the life of St. Anthony of Egypt.
Explain why people went to the desert (to escape a worldly church).
Compare living in the world vs. living in a monastery.
Apply the value of silence and prayer.
Analyze the benefits (preservation of scripture) and dangers (isolation) of monasticism.
Interpret the Benedictine Rule (Ora et Labora - Pray and Work).
Connect monasticism to the preservation of literacy in the Dark Ages.
Explain the difference between Eremitic (hermit) and Cenobitic (community) monks.
Construct a critique of the two-tiered spirituality (monks vs. laity).
Evaluate the impact of monasticism on Western civilization.
Defend the biblical call to be 'in the world but not of it'.
Produce a reflection on the disciplines of solitude and simplicity.

BIB.4.1.4.t: Identify an Apologist as someone who explains why Jesus is true.
Name Justin Martyr as a wise teacher.
Recall that people told lies about Christians.
Observe that we can use words to defend Jesus.
Summarize the lies told about Christians (cannibalism, atheism).
Explain how Justin Martyr defended the faith to the Emperor.
Compare fighting with swords vs. fighting with truth.
Apply the need to know *why* we believe.
Analyze the dialogue with Trypho the Jew.
Interpret the use of Greek philosophy (Logos) to explain Christ.
Connect the early apologists to modern apologetics.
Construct a summary of the key arguments in the 'Apology' of Justin.
Evaluate the risks and rewards of using secular philosophy to explain faith.
Defend the rationality of the Christian worldview as presented by the Fathers.
Synthesize the development of the Rule of Faith.

BIB.4.1.5.t: Identify the Apostolic Fathers as men who knew the disciples.
Name Polycarp as a brave old man who loved Jesus.
Recall that they wrote letters to encourage churches.
Observe that the church continued after the Bible was finished.
Summarize the story of Polycarp's martyrdom.
Explain who Clement of Rome and Ignatius were.
Compare the writings of the Apostles (Bible) with the Fathers (Helpful but not inspired).
Apply the lesson of standing firm in faith from Ignatius.
Analyze the 'Didache' as an early church manual.
Interpret the letters of Ignatius regarding the role of the bishop.
Connect the Apostolic Fathers to the preservation of the New Testament text.
Explain the transition from oral tradition to written record.
Construct a timeline of the 1st and 2nd century church leaders.
Evaluate the theology of Clement regarding justification.
Defend the historical continuity of the church.
Synthesize the apologetic arguments used by early writers against paganism.

BIB.4.1.6.t: Identify a Council as a big meeting of church leaders.
Name the Creed as a statement of what we believe.
Recall that they agreed Jesus is fully God.
Recite a simple line from the Apostles' Creed.
Summarize the Council of Nicea (325 AD).
Explain why it is important that Jesus is 'of one substance' with the Father.
Compare a Creed with a Hymn.
Analyze the debate between Arius (Jesus is created) and Athanasius (Jesus is God).
Interpret the Nicene Creed's clauses on the Holy Spirit.
Connect the Council of Chalcedon to the doctrine of the Hypostatic Union.
Construct a historical overview of the first four Ecumenical Councils.
Evaluate the necessity of precise theological language.
Defend the orthodoxy of the Nicene Creed against modern heresies.
Produce a study on Athanasius 'Contra Mundum' (Against the World).

BIB.4.2.1.t: Identify John Wycliffe as the 'Morning Star'.
Name Jan Hus as a brave preacher.
Recall that they wanted the Bible in their own language.
Observe that they were treated badly for speaking truth.
Summarize the life of John Wycliffe.
Explain why the church didn't want people reading the Bible.
Compare Wycliffe's 'Poor Priests' with rich bishops.
Apply the courage of Jan Hus at the stake.
Analyze Wycliffe's translation of the Bible into English.
Interpret the Council of Constance (burning of Hus).
Connect these men to the later work of Martin Luther.
Explain the concept of 'Sola Scriptura' before the Reformation.
Construct a timeline of dissent leading to 1517.
Evaluate the Lollard movement in England.
Defend the right of the laity to read Scripture.
Produce an essay on the cost of reforming the church.

BIB.4.2.2.t: Identify that people started schools to study God.
Name Thomas Aquinas as a smart thinker.
Recall that we should love God with our minds.
Observe old universities like Oxford and Paris.
Compare learning in a monastery vs. learning in a university.
Apply the use of logic to faith.
Analyze the goal of Scholasticism (systematizing theology).
Interpret Anselm's 'Cur Deus Homo' (Why God became Man).
Connect Aquinas' 'Summa Theologica' to Catholic doctrine.
Construct a summary of the Five Ways (Aquinas' arguments for God).
Evaluate the synthesis of Greek Philosophy and Biblical Theology.
Defend the substitutionary atonement articulated by Anselm.
Synthesize the intellectual achievements of the High Middle Ages.

BIB.4.2.3.t: Identify that the big church split in two.
Name the West (Catholic) and the East (Orthodox).
Observe that they disagreed on rules and leaders.
Explain the difference between the Pope (West) and Patriarch (East).
Compare the Latin church with the Greek church.
Locate Rome and Constantinople on a map.
Interpret the political and cultural divide (Latin vs. Greek).
Connect the Crusades to the deepening of the split.
Construct a comparison of Orthodox and Catholic theology.
Evaluate the 'Filioque' controversy regarding the Trinity.
Defend the importance of unity in truth.
Produce a study on the Fourth Crusade's sack of Constantinople.

BIB.4.2.4.t: Identify the Pope as the leader of the church in Rome.
Name Rome as the main city.
Recall that Peter and Paul died in Rome.
Observe that the church became very powerful.
Summarize how the Bishop of Rome became the Pope.
Explain the story of Leo the Great stopping Attila the Hun.
Compare the authority of the Bible with the authority of the Pope.
Categorize the hierarchy: Pope, Cardinal, Bishop, Priest.
Interpret Gregory the Great's influence on the medieval church.
Connect the fall of the Roman Empire to the rise of Church power.
Explain the Donation of Constantine (and its forgery).
Construct a historical evaluation of the accumulation of Papal power.
Evaluate the conflict between Popes and Kings (Investiture Controversy).
Defend the Protestant rejection of the Papacy.
Synthesize the mixing of temporal and spiritual power.

BIB.4.3.1.t: Identify John Calvin as a teacher in Geneva.
Recall that he taught us about God's great power.
Observe that Geneva became a city of Bible study.
Summarize Calvin's emphasis on the glory of God.
Compare Luther (the starter) with Calvin (the organizer).
Categorize Geneva as a refuge for Protestants.
Analyze the impact of Calvin's 'Institutes of the Christian Religion'.
Interpret Calvin's view of the Lord's Supper (Spiritual Presence).
Connect Knox, the Puritans, and Pilgrims to Calvin's influence.
Explain the sovereignty of God in salvation.
Construct a profile of Calvin as a pastor and theologian.
Evaluate the affair of Michael Servetus.
Defend the doctrine of Predestination as biblical.
Synthesize the legacy of Calvinism in Western history.

BIB.4.3.2.t: Identify Martin Luther as a monk with a hammer.
Name the 95 Theses on the door.
Recall that Luther said we are saved by faith, not money.
Observe that Luther translated the Bible for everyone.
Summarize the story of the lightning storm and Luther's vow.
Explain what an 'Indulgence' was (paying for forgiveness).
Compare Luther's view of salvation with the Pope's view.
Apply the courage of 'Here I Stand'.
Connect the printing press to the spread of Luther's ideas.
Explain the concept of the 'Priesthood of all Believers'.
Construct a theology of the Cross vs. theology of Glory.
Evaluate Luther's later writings and errors.
Defend the necessity of the breach with Rome.
Synthesize the impact of the German Bible.

BIB.4.3.3.t: Name Grace Alone, Faith Alone, Christ Alone.
Recall that Scripture Alone is our rule.
Observe that all is for God's Glory Alone.
Summarize the meaning of each Sola.
Explain why 'Alone' is the most important word.
Compare adding to Jesus vs. Jesus Alone.
Apply 'Soli Deo Gloria' to school and play.
Analyze how each Sola countered a Catholic error.
Interpret Ephesians 2:8-9 in light of the Solas.
Explain the sufficiency of Christ (Solus Christus).
Construct a systematic defense of the Five Solas.
Evaluate modern evangelicalism through the lens of the Solas.
Defend 'Sola Fide' as the article on which the church stands or falls.
Produce an essay on the interconnectedness of the five doctrines.

BIB.4.3.4.t: Identify Zwingli as a leader in Switzerland.
Name the Anabaptists as people who wanted to be baptized again.
Recall that they wanted to obey the Bible exactly.
Observe that they were persecuted by everyone.
Summarize Zwingli's disagreement with Luther (Marburg Colloquy).
Explain why Anabaptists believed in believer's baptism.
Compare the Magisterial Reformers (church/state) with Radicals (separate).
Apply the courage to stand for conviction.
Analyze the 'Affair of the Sausages' (Zwingli breaking fast).
Interpret the Anabaptist view of the separation of church and state.
Connect the Amish and Mennonites to this movement.
Explain the tragedy of Protestants persecuting Protestants.
Construct a comparison of Lutheran, Reformed, and Anabaptist theology.
Evaluate the pacifism of the Radical Reformation.
Defend the concept of a 'Believers' Church'.
Produce a study on the Munster Rebellion vs. peaceful Anabaptists.

BIB.5.1.1.t: Identify the Buddha as a teacher who sat under a tree.
Name him as a man who wanted to stop sadness.
Recall that he taught people to be calm and kind.
Summarize the story of Siddhartha Gautama (the prince who left home).
Explain the idea of 'Nirvana' (blowing out the candle of desire).
Compare the Buddha (a man seeking truth) with Jesus (the Truth).
Apply the value of peace but with a different hope.
Analyze the Four Noble Truths (Life is suffering, caused by desire).
Interpret the Eightfold Path as a way of self-salvation.
Connect Buddhism to its roots in Hinduism (Karma/Reincarnation).
Construct a critique of the Buddhist view of suffering (illusion/detachment).
Evaluate the goal of extinguishing the self vs. glorifying God.
Defend the reality of suffering and the Christian response (Redemption).
Synthesize the differences between Theravada and Mahayana Buddhism.

BIB.5.2.1.t: Identify that we should do the right thing even if it's hard.
Observe that sometimes we want to do what is easy, not right.
Summarize 'The Greatest Good for the Greatest Number' (Utilitarianism).
Explain why the end doesn't justify the means.
Compare following rules (Duty) with being a good person (Character).
Apply decision-making to a difficult situation.
Interpret Virtue Ethics (becoming a certain type of person).
Connect Christian ethics to the character of God (we do good because He is good).
Construct a critique of Utilitarianism using human rights.
Evaluate Kantian ethics (Categorical Imperative) from a Christian view.
Defend Virtue Ethics as closest to the biblical idea of Sanctification.
Produce an essay on a complex bioethical issue (e.g., genetic engineering).

BIB.5.2.2.t: Identify that God decides what is right and wrong.
Name the Bible as our rule book.
Recall that doing good makes God happy.
Observe that people who don't know God still know right from wrong.
Summarize why we need God to have real rules.
Explain that 'Secular' means leaving God out.
Compare 'Because God says so' with 'Because I feel like it'.
Apply the Ten Commandments to modern life.
Analyze the Euthyphro Dilemma (Is it good because God loves it?).
Connect the idea of human rights to the Image of God.
Explain Moral Relativism ('That's true for you').
Construct a defense of Objective Morality.
Evaluate Evolutionary Ethics (morality as survival instinct).
Defend the consistency of Divine Command Theory.
Synthesize the relationship between Law and Love.

BIB.5.3.1.t: Identify Hinduism as a very old religion from India.
Name 'Karma' as the idea that what you do comes back to you.
Recall that they believe people are born again and again.
Observe statues of gods with many arms.
Explain what the Vedas are (holy books).
Compare the one God of the Bible with the millions of gods in Hinduism.
Identify the caste system (different levels of people).
Analyze the concept of Brahman (Ultimate Reality) vs. Atman (Soul).
Interpret the goal of Moksha (escaping the cycle of rebirth).
Connect the practice of Yoga to Hindu philosophy.
Explain the cyclical view of history vs. the biblical linear view.
Construct a critique of Pantheism (God is all).
Evaluate the problem of suffering in Hinduism (Karma) vs. Christianity (Fall/Redemption).
Defend the distinct personhood of God and humans.
Synthesize the cultural impact of Hinduism on the West (New Age).

BIB.5.3.2.t: Identify temples where people bring fruit and flowers.
Name cows as special animals in India.
Recall that they use statues to help them pray.
Explain what an 'Avatar' is (a god coming down in a body).
Compare an idol with the living God.
Apply the biblical command against idolatry.
Interpret the role of the Guru.
Connect the Ganges river to spiritual cleansing.
Explain the difference between Polytheism and Monotheism.
Construct a comparison of the Incarnation of Christ vs. Hindu Avatars.
Evaluate the social ethics of the Caste System.
Defend the resurrection of the body against the absorption of the soul.
Produce a reflection on the uniqueness of Christ's sacrifice.

BIB.5.4.1.t: Identify Muslims as people who follow Islam.
Name the Mosque as their place of prayer.
Recall that they believe in one God called Allah.
Observe that they pray on mats.
Compare Jesus (Son of God) with Isa (Jesus as a Prophet in Islam).
Identify Mecca as the most special city for Muslims.
Analyze the claim that the Bible has been corrupted.
Interpret the Shahada ('There is no God but Allah...').
Connect the history of Ishmael to Arab identity.
Explain the difference between Sunni and Shia Muslims.
Construct a critique of the Islamic dilemma regarding the Bible's authority.
Evaluate the Islamic denial of the Crucifixion and Trinity.
Defend the historical reliability of the Gospels vs. the Quran.
Synthesize the theological differences regarding the nature of God (Love vs. Will).

BIB.5.4.2.t: Identify the Quran as the holy book of Islam.
Name prayer and giving as things they do.
Recall that they fast (don't eat) during Ramadan.
Observe beautiful writing (calligraphy) in their art.
Summarize the Five Pillars (Faith, Prayer, Alms, Fasting, Pilgrimage).
Explain what Hajj is (trip to Mecca).
Compare the Bible's structure with the Quran's structure.
Categorize the requirements for salvation in Islam (scales of good vs. bad).
Analyze the concept of Jihad (inner struggle and outer war).
Interpret the role of the Hadith (sayings of Muhammad).
Connect the ritual washing (Wudu) to OT ceremonial laws.
Explain the Islamic view of Paradise.
Construct a comparison of the God of the Quran and the God of the Bible.
Evaluate the concept of Sharia Law and its implications.
Defend Salvation by Grace against Salvation by Works/Pillars.
Produce an essay on the challenge of evangelism to Muslims.

BIB.5.5.1.t: Identify that Jewish people believe in one God.
Recall that they respect God's name very much.
Summarize the importance of the Shema ('Hear O Israel').
Explain what the Talmud is (writings of the teachers).
Compare the Christian view of God (Trinity) with the Jewish view (Monotheism).
Apply respect for the Jewish roots of the Christian faith.
Analyze the concept of Mitzvot (Commandments) as a way of life.
Interpret the role of the Rabbi vs. the Priest.
Connect the Oral Law to the traditions Jesus debated.
Explain the Jewish view of sin and atonement without a Temple.
Construct a comparison of Soteriology (Salvation by Law/Heritage vs. Grace).
Evaluate the historical reliability of the Talmudic traditions.
Defend the Christian reading of Isaiah 53 against modern Jewish interpretations.
Produce a study on the concept of 'God's Chosen People'.

BIB.5.5.2.t: Name the Old Testament as the Bible Jewish people read.
Recall that they worship the One True God.
Observe a Menorah or Star of David.
Summarize the story of Abraham as the father of the Jewish people.
Explain that Jewish people are still waiting for the Messiah.
Compare a Synagogue service with a Church service.
Identify the Torah as the most holy books for Jews.
Analyze the transition from Temple Judaism to Rabbinic Judaism (AD 70).
Interpret the continuity of the moral law vs. the discontinuity of the ceremonial law.
Connect the Old Testament prophecies to Jewish expectations today.
Explain the difference between Orthodox, Conservative, and Reform Judaism.
Construct a theology of Israel and the Church (Covenant vs. Dispensational views).
Evaluate the Jewish rejection of the Trinity (Shema interpretation).
Defend the Messiahship of Jesus using the Hebrew Bible.
Synthesize the shared heritage and distinct divergences of the two faiths.

BIB.5.5.3.t: Identify Shabbat (Sabbath) as a day of rest.
Recall that some foods are not allowed (Kosher).
Summarize the rules of keeping Kosher (dietary laws).
Explain the meaning of Bar/Bat Mitzvah (becoming an adult).
Compare Sunday worship with Saturday Sabbath.
Categorize the major Jewish holidays and what they remember.
Analyze the purpose of the dietary laws in Leviticus (separation).
Interpret the symbolism of the Passover Seder.
Connect the Jewish festivals to the life of Jesus.
Explain the significance of the Western Wall.
Construct a theological evaluation of Sabbath-keeping for Christians.
Evaluate the legalism vs. devotion in strict observance.
Defend the freedom of the Christian from the ceremonial law (Acts 15).
Synthesize the prophetic fulfillment of the Feasts.

BIB.5.6.1.t: Identify a wedding as a promise before God.
Name Baptism as a special church event for believers.
Recall that families celebrate when babies are born.
Observe that different religions have different parties.
Summarize the meaning of Christian Baptism.
Explain what a Bar Mitzvah is for Jewish boys.
Compare a Christian wedding vow with a legal contract.
Categorize rites of passage (growing up ceremonies).
Analyze the covenantal nature of Christian marriage.
Interpret the symbolism of water in baptism and other rituals.
Connect confirmation/profession of faith to personal ownership of belief.
Explain how rituals help communities stay together.
Construct a theology of the family based on Genesis 2 and Ephesians 5.
Evaluate the secular view of marriage (contract) vs. covenant.
Defend the definition of marriage as between one man and one woman.
Synthesize the sociological function of ritual with theological meaning.

BIB.5.6.2.t: Name Heaven as the home of believers.
Recall that we will see Jesus when we die.
Observe that funerals are sad but we have hope.
Summarize the Christian hope of Resurrection.
Compare a Christian funeral with a pagan one.
Apply 1 Thessalonians 4 ('We do not grieve as those who have no hope').
Analyze the different views of the intermediate state.
Interpret the concept of 'Sheol/Hades' vs. Heaven/Hell.
Connect the Resurrection of Jesus to our future resurrection.
Explain the difference between Annihilationism and Eternal Conscious Torment.
Construct a biblical theology of death as an enemy that is defeated.
Defend the reality of Hell and the justice of God.
Produce a reflection on 'O Death, where is your sting?'

BIB.6.1.1.t: Identify what God wants me to do today.
Name a way to obey the verse.
Recall that the Bible is for us, even though it's old.
Ask 'How can I be like Jesus?'
Summarize the difference between 'Then' (Bible times) and 'Now'.
Explain that we must understand it before we apply it.
Compare a cultural custom (sandals) with the principle (humility).
Apply a specific application to school or family.
Analyze the 'Principlizing Bridge' (finding the timeless truth).
Interpret commands that are cultural vs. universal.
Connect the Indicative (Who you are) to the Imperative (What you do).
Explain the danger of legalistic application.
Construct a culturally relevant application of an ancient text.
Evaluate modern ethical dilemmas using biblical principles.
Defend the relevance of the Old Testament for modern living.
Produce a devotional or sermon outline applying a text to a specific audience.

BIB.6.1.2.t: Identify the beginning, middle, and end of a story.
Recall that stories have a shape.
Summarize the outline of a chapter.
Explain how paragraphs group ideas together.
Compare the structure of a Poem (lines) with a Letter (paragraphs).
Interpret the logical flow words (Therefore, But, For).
Connect the structure of a book to its message.
Construct a sentence diagram of a complex Pauline sentence.
Evaluate the macro-structure of a book (e.g., Matthew's 5 discourses).
Defend an interpretation based on the grammatical structure.
Synthesize the syntax and the theology of a passage.

BIB.6.1.3.t: Identify that the Bible was written by hand a long time ago.
Name the Scribes who copied it carefully.
Recall that we can trust the Bible we have.
Observe the footnotes in a Bible.
Summarize how we got our English Bible from Hebrew and Greek.
Explain that sometimes copiers made tiny spelling mistakes.
Compare the number of Bible copies with other old books (like Homer).
Apply confidence in the Word of God.
Analyze why some Bibles have brackets around verses (e.g., Mark 16).
Interpret the difference between a 'variant' and an 'error'.
Connect the Dead Sea Scrolls to the accuracy of the OT.
Explain the reliability of the transmission process.
Construct a defense of the text based on the vast number of manuscripts.
Evaluate the impact of textual variants on doctrine (none affected).
Perform simple comparisons of translation philosophies (KJV vs. ESV vs. NIV).
Synthesize the history of the textus receptus vs. critical text.

BIB.6.1.4.t: Identify what a story teaches about God.
Recall that all stories point to one big Truth.
Observe how God acts the same way in different stories.
Summarize the doctrine taught in a passage.
Explain how a verse fits with the rest of the Bible.
Compare a specific command with a general principle.
Categorize a passage under a doctrine (e.g., God, Man, Sin).
Analyze the theological implications of a text.
Interpret a narrative text to find the theological principle.
Connect Exegesis (the text) to Systematic Theology (the doctrine).
Construct a theological statement based on exegetical work.
Evaluate a systematic doctrine based on biblical evidence.
Defend a doctrine using proof texts correctly handled.
Synthesize the results of word studies, grammar, and history into a doctrinal conclusion.

BIB.6.1.5.t: Identify big words in the Bible (Grace, Sin, Faith).
Name a Bible dictionary as a helper.
Recall that words mean special things.
Observe that the same word can be used in different places.
Summarize the definition of key terms like 'Justification'.
Explain that the Bible was written in Hebrew and Greek.
Compare how a word is used in different verses.
Apply a Strong's Concordance number to find a definition.
Analyze the 'Semantic Range' of a word (it can mean different things).
Interpret a word based on how the specific author uses it.
Connect a Greek word (like Agape) to its definition.
Explain the danger of the 'Root Fallacy' (etymology is not meaning).
Construct a word study on a key theological term.
Evaluate the usage of a word in the Septuagint (LXX) vs. NT.
Defend the importance of precise definitions in theology.
Produce a study on a concept (like 'Flesh' in Paul) using a lexicon.

BIB.6.2.1.t: Identify that the Bible tells one big true story.
Name the Bible as the best helper to understand the Bible.
Recall that God never contradicts Himself.
Observe that the New Testament helps us understand the Old Testament.
Explain that clear verses help us understand hard verses.
Compare two verses on the same topic to get the full picture.
Apply cross-references to find other verses.
Analyze apparent contradictions (e.g., Paul vs. James) using harmonization.
Interpret obscure passages in light of systematic theology.
Connect OT types to NT antitypes.
Explain the unity of the Bible.
Construct a systematic theology on a topic using the whole Bible.
Evaluate how the Apostles interpreted the OT (hermeneutics of the Apostles).
Defend the internal consistency of the Scriptures.
Produce a study reconciling difficult parallel passages (e.g., Kings/Chronicles or Gospels).

BIB.6.2.2.t: Identify that God used men to write the Bible.
Name the person who wrote the book (like Luke).
Recall that the writer wanted to tell us something specific.
Ask 'What did the writer want us to know?'
Summarize the main point the author was making.
Explain that we can't make the Bible mean whatever we want.
Compare what I *feel* about a verse with what the author *said*.
Apply the idea that there is one meaning but many applications.
Analyze the 'Occasion' for writing (Why did Paul write Galatians?).
Interpret the difference between Authorial Intent and Reader Response.
Connect the human author's intent to the Divine Author's intent.
Explain the concept of 'Dual Authorship' (Holy Spirit and Man).
Construct a thesis on the intent of a specific book.
Evaluate postmodern views that 'the author is dead'.
Defend the objective meaning of Scripture.
Synthesize the human personality of the author with the doctrine of Inspiration.

BIB.6.2.3.t: Identify a story vs. a song.
Name a letter (Epistle) vs. a rule (Law).
Recall that the Bible has different kinds of writing.
Observe that poetry uses picture words.
Summarize the difference between History (Kings) and Prophecy (Isaiah).
Explain that a Parable is a made-up story to teach a truth.
Compare reading a Psalm with reading a Commandment.
Categorize Bible books by their genre.
Analyze the rules for interpreting Apocalyptic literature (Daniel/Revelation).
Interpret Hebrew Poetry (recognizing parallelism, not literalism).
Connect the genre to the author's purpose.
Explain why Wisdom Literature (Proverbs) are probabilities, not promises.
Construct a hermeneutic for Epistolary literature (occasional nature).
Evaluate the difference between Descriptive (Narrative) and Prescriptive (Didactic) texts.
Defend the historicity of Narrative against 'myth' interpretations.
Synthesize genre analysis into the study of a specific book.

BIB.6.2.4.t: Identify that God told us more and more over time.
Name Jesus as the final word from God.
Recall that Adam knew a little, but we know a lot.
Observe how the story grows like a tree.
Summarize the growth from the Garden to the City.
Explain that the Old Testament is the shadow, and Jesus is the substance.
Compare the partial knowledge of Moses with the full knowledge in Christ.
Apply the blessing of having the whole Bible.
Analyze the unfolding of the Covenant (Seed -> Land -> King -> World).
Interpret the 'Mystery' that was hidden but is now revealed (Ephesians 3).
Connect the Levitical sacrifices to the finality of the Cross.
Explain why we don't follow ceremonial laws anymore.
Construct a timeline of theological development.
Evaluate Dispensational vs. Covenantal views of progression.
Defend the superiority of the New Covenant revelation (Hebrews 1).
Synthesize the organic unity of the Bible from seed to fruit.

BIB.6.2.5.t: Identify that the Bible tells us true things that really happened.
Name the writer (like Moses or Paul) of a book.
Recall that words have specific meanings.
Observe that we read the Bible just like we read other true stories.
Summarize the 'plain meaning' of the text.
Explain that we must understand what it meant to the first readers.
Compare a literal reading with a made-up meaning.
Apply the rule: 'If the plain sense makes sense, seek no other sense.'
Analyze the historical setting of a book (author, date, audience).
Interpret the text according to the rules of grammar.
Connect the meaning of a passage to the history of that time.
Explain why we avoid allegorizing historical narratives.
Construct a defense of the Grammatical-Historical hermeneutic.
Perform research on the cultural background of a passage to illuminate meaning.
Synthesize the relationship between history and theology.

BIB.6.2.6.t: Identify what happened right before a story.
Name the book that a verse comes from.
Recall that we shouldn't pick verses like magic tricks.
Observe that stories have a beginning, middle, and end.
Summarize the paragraph surrounding a verse.
Explain that taking things 'out of context' changes the meaning.
Compare the Immediate Context (surrounding verses) with the Broad Context (whole book).
Apply context to correct a wrong idea (e.g., 'I can do all things' in Phil 4).
Analyze the logical flow of an argument in an epistle.
Interpret a difficult verse by looking at the whole chapter.
Connect a single passage to the overall theme of the book.
Explain the three circles of context: Immediate, Book, and Canonical.
Construct a context chart for a specific book.
Evaluate popular misinterpretations based on isolation of verses.
Defend the principle that context determines meaning.
Produce an exegetical outline tracing the author's thought process.

BIB.7.1.1.t: Order the pictures of Adam, Noah, Moses, and Jesus.
Identify that the Bible covers a very, very long time.
Recall that Jesus came at exactly the right time.
Use a timeline string to see who lived first.
Summarize the main eras: Creation, Patriarchs, Exodus, Kings, Exile.
Explain the difference between BC (Before Christ) and AD (Anno Domini).
Compare the time of David (1000 BC) to the time of the Exile (586 BC).
Calculate how many years ago Jesus lived.
Interpret the 480 years mentioned in 1 Kings 6:1.
Connect biblical events to fixed dates in history (e.g., Battle of Carchemish).
Explain the debate between the Early Date and Late Date of the Exodus.
Construct a synchronized timeline of Hebrew Kings and Assyrian/Babylonian rulers.
Evaluate the challenges of biblical chronology (Masoretic vs. Septuagint numbers).
Defend the historicity of the biblical timeline against minimalism.
Produce a study on the significance of the '400 Silent Years'.

BIB.7.1.2.t: Identify God as the one who spoke the world into being.
Name the sun and moon as lights God made, not gods to worship.
Recall that other people believed scary stories about monsters making the world.
Express thanks that our God is good and loving.
Summarize the difference between believing in one God (Monotheism) and many gods (Polytheism).
Explain that Genesis says humans are special rulers, not slaves to gods.
Compare the peace of the Garden of Eden with the violence of other creation myths.
Categorize the stars as creation, not controllers of our fate.
Analyze the Enuma Elish and its contrast with Genesis 1.
Interpret Genesis 1 as a 'polemic' (argument) against pagan worldviews.
Connect the biblical view of nature (demythologized) to the rise of science.
Explain the concept of the 'Cosmic Temple' in ancient thought.
Construct a worldview comparison: Ancient Paganism vs. Biblical Theism vs. Modern Materialism.
Evaluate the 'chaos monster' motif (Leviathan/Rahab) in Scripture vs. ANE mythology.
Defend the transcendence and immanence of God against pantheism.
Produce an essay on how the biblical worldview dignifies humanity.

BIB.7.1.3.t: Identify that the Old Testament was written in Hebrew.
Name 'Shalom' as a Hebrew word for peace.
Recall that Jesus spoke a language called Aramaic.
Observe what Hebrew letters look like (reading right to left).
Summarize how we got our English Bible from the original languages.
Explain that some parts of Daniel were written in Aramaic.
Compare the look of English letters to Hebrew letters.
Recognize that translation involves choosing the best words.
Analyze the importance of the Dead Sea Scrolls.
Interpret the difference between a 'word-for-word' and 'thought-for-thought' translation.
Connect the Ugaritic language to understanding difficult Hebrew poetry.
Explain why the Jews translated the OT into Greek (the Septuagint).
Construct a basic word study using a concordance.
Evaluate how knowing original languages enriches theology (e.g., 'Chesed' - lovingkindness).
Defend the preservation of the biblical text through history.
Synthesize the impact of Aramaic as the 'lingua franca' of the ancient Near East.

BIB.7.1.4.t: Identify rules as things that keep us safe.
Name the Ten Commandments as God's special rules.
Recall that kings in Bible times made rules on big stones.
Observe that God's laws are fair and good.
Summarize the idea of 'eye for an eye' (fairness, not revenge).
Explain what a 'treaty' is (an agreement between a king and people).
Compare the harsh laws of Hammurabi with the laws of Moses.
Apply the idea that God is our King and we are His people.
Analyze the suzerain-vassal treaty structure in Deuteronomy.
Interpret the difference between apodictic (absolute) and casuistic (case) law.
Connect the blessings and curses of the Law to ancient treaty formats.
Explain how the Mosaic law protected servants and women uniquely in the ancient world.
Construct a comparison of ANE law codes and the Torah regarding the value of human life.
Evaluate the 'lex talionis' (law of retaliation) as a limit on vengeance.
Perform research on the Hittite treaties of the 2nd millennium BC.
Synthesize the uniqueness of Israel's law being grounded in the character of Yahweh.

BIB.7.1.5.t: Identify Egypt as the land of Pyramids and the Nile River.
Name Abraham's first home as the city of Ur.
Recall that people in Bible times wrote on clay and stone.
Observe pictures of ancient ziggurats (tall towers).
Summarize the geography of the Fertile Crescent.
Explain how the Nile River helped Egypt grow food.
Compare the life of an Israelite shepherd with an Egyptian city dweller.
Locate Babylon, Assyria, and Egypt on a Bible map.
Analyze the geopolitical struggle between the empires of the North (Assyria/Babylon) and the South (Egypt).
Interpret the cultural significance of the Code of Hammurabi.
Connect the plagues of Egypt to specific Egyptian false gods.
Explain the significance of the 'cradle of civilization' for biblical history.
Construct a profile of the Assyrian war machine and its impact on Israel.
Evaluate the archaeological evidence for Israel's presence in Egypt.
Defend the historical reliability of the biblical account amidst ANE records.
Synthesize the rise and fall of ANE empires with the prophecies of Daniel.

BIB.7.2.1.t: Name a boat sailing on the sea.
Recall that Paul traveled to tell people about Jesus.
Observe that it was safe to travel then.
Explain how good roads helped spread the Gospel.
Compare travel then (walking/sailing) with travel now.
Identify the lack of pirates on the sea.
Analyze the extent of the Roman road network.
Interpret the phrase 'in the fullness of time' regarding Roman infrastructure.
Connect the common Greek language (Koine) to ease of communication.
Explain the role of Roman colonies like Philippi.
Construct a map of Paul's journeys utilizing Roman routes.
Evaluate the cost and danger of travel despite the peace.
Defend the providential timing of Christ's birth.
Synthesize the material conditions that facilitated the early church's growth.

BIB.7.2.2.t: Recall that Romans wanted people to worship the Emperor.
Observe that Christians said 'Jesus is Lord'.
Explain why Christians got in trouble (refusing to worship Caesar).
Compare the true God with idols.
Analyze the syncretism of the Roman world.
Interpret the political nature of worshiping Caesar.
Connect the persecution in Revelation to the Imperial Cult.
Explain the 'atheism' charge against Christians (no visible god).
Construct a contrast between the Kingdom of Caesar and the Kingdom of Christ.
Evaluate the mystery religions of the time.
Defend the exclusivity of the Christian confession.
Synthesize the cultural pressure to conform with the call to holiness.

BIB.7.2.3.t: Identify a master and a servant.
Name a rich person and a poor person.
Recall that Jesus loves everyone the same.
Observe that Romans had strict rules about who was important.
Summarize the difference between a Citizen and a Non-Citizen.
Explain that many people were slaves in Rome.
Compare the way Rome treated people with how the Church did.
Interpret Paul's teaching on 'neither slave nor free'.
Connect social status to the seating at the Lord's Supper.
Explain the role of women in the Roman world vs. the Church.
Construct a profile of a typical Roman household.
Evaluate the radical nature of Christian fellowship.
Defend the biblical undermining of the institution of slavery.
Synthesize the sociology of the early church.

BIB.7.2.4.t: Identify men thinking and talking in Athens.
Name Paul talking to thinkers on Mars Hill.
Recall that people wanted to know how to be happy.
Summarize Epicureans (seek pleasure) and Stoics (be tough).
Explain that they didn't know the true God.
Compare wisdom of the world with wisdom of God.
Interpret the Stoic view of Logos vs. John's Logos.
Connect Gnosticism to Greek thought (spirit good, matter bad).
Explain the pursuit of 'Ataraxia' (peace of mind).
Construct a comparison of Christian ethics with Stoic ethics.
Evaluate the emptiness of philosophy without Christ.
Defend the resurrection against Greek skepticism.
Synthesize the interaction of the Gospel with the intellectual world.

BIB.7.3.1.t: Identify the Temple in Jesus' time.
Recall that they didn't like Jesus.
Summarize the difference between Pharisees and Sadducees.
Compare the Zealots (fighters) with the Essenes (monks).
Connect the Sadducees to the Temple power.
Explain the Essene community at Qumran (Dead Sea Scrolls).
Construct a profile of First Century Judaism.
Evaluate the expectation of a political Messiah.
Defend Jesus' interaction with the Law vs. Tradition.
Synthesize the diversity within Judaism at the time of Christ.

BIB.7.3.2.t: Identify a Synagogue as a church for Jews.
Recall that they read the Bible every Sabbath.
Observe Jesus teaching in the synagogue.
Summarize what happened in a Synagogue service (Reading, Prayer).
Explain that the Temple was for sacrifice, Synagogue for learning.
Compare a Synagogue ruler with a Priest.
Analyze the role of the Sanhedrin in the trial of Jesus.
Interpret the Diaspora (Jews living outside Israel).
Connect the Synagogue to the pattern of early Christian worship.
Construct a diagram of the Sanhedrin's structure.
Evaluate the legal authority of Jewish courts under Rome.
Defend the importance of the Synagogue in preserving the faith.
Synthesize the transition from Temple-based to Torah-based religion.

BIB.7.3.3.t: Recall that God gave them holidays to remember Him.
Compare the Sabbath (rest) with a yearly festival.
Analyze the prophetic meaning of the Feasts.
Interpret Jesus as the fulfillment of the Passover.
Connect the outpouring of the Spirit to the Feast of Weeks.
Explain the Day of Atonement (Yom Kippur).
Construct a calendar of the Jewish Year.
Evaluate the historical context of Hanukkah (Maccabees).
Defend the Typology of the Feasts pointing to Christ.
Synthesize the cycle of remembrance in Jewish life.

BIB.7.3.4.t: Identify that people were waiting for a King.
Recall that they wanted him to fight the Romans.
Summarize why they were surprised by Jesus (He was humble).
Compare a warrior king with a suffering servant.
Connect Daniel's prophecies to 1st Century hopes.
Explain the concept of the 'Age to Come'.
Construct a profile of the different messianic expectations.
Evaluate why Judas might have betrayed Jesus (disappointment).
Defend Jesus' redefinition of the Messiahship.
Synthesize the Jewish roots of Christian eschatology.

BIB.8.1.1.t: Name the Holy Spirit as the Helper.
Observe that people from many nations heard the Gospel.
Explain why they spoke in other languages (reversing Babel).
Compare the fear of the disciples before Pentecost with their courage after.
Identify the birth of the Church.
Analyze the sermon of Peter (using OT prophecy).
Connect the Spirit to the empowerment for witness.
Explain the role of the Spirit in conviction of sin.
Construct a theology of the Holy Spirit’s role in missions.
Evaluate the difference between the indwelling and the filling of the Spirit.
Defend the personhood of the Holy Spirit.
Synthesize the link between Pentecost and the Great Commission.

BIB.8.1.2.t: Identify that the first Christians shared their food.
Name Stephen as the first martyr.
Recall that they prayed together every day.
Observe that the leaders were put in jail.
Summarize the life of the early church (Acts 2:42).
Explain why Stephen was stoned (he spoke truth).
Compare the generosity of Barnabas with Ananias and Sapphira.
Identify the scattering of the believers.
Analyze the prayer of the church under threat (Acts 4).
Interpret the appointment of Deacons (Acts 6) to solve problems.
Connect persecution to the spread of the Gospel (Samaria).
Evaluate the tension between Jewish tradition and the new faith.
Defend the historical reality of the early church's socialism (voluntary vs. forced).
Synthesize the blood of the martyrs as the seed of the church.

BIB.8.1.3.t: Identify Paul traveling on a boat.
Name Barnabas and Silas as helpers.
Observe lines on a map showing where he went.
Summarize the pattern: Synagogue first, then Gentiles.
Explain why Paul went to big cities.
Compare the reception in Berea (noble) vs. Thessalonica (hostile).
Analyze Paul’s speech at the Areopagus (Athens).
Interpret the riot in Ephesus (Diana of the Ephesians).
Connect the planting of churches to the writing of letters.
Explain the role of the Holy Spirit in directing the mission.
Construct a map of the three journeys.
Evaluate Paul’s contextualization of the Gospel for Greeks vs. Jews.
Defend the strategy of urban church planting.
Synthesize the cost of discipleship seen in Paul’s sufferings.

BIB.8.1.4.t: Identify that non-Jewish people believed in Jesus.
Name Peter’s vision of the sheet with animals.
Recall that God loves everyone, not just one group.
Summarize the question: Do Gentiles need to become Jews first?
Explain the decision (Saved by grace, not law).
Compare the Old Testament rules (food/circumcision) with New Testament freedom.
Identify James as the leader of the Council.
Analyze the testimony of Peter and Paul.
Interpret the letter sent to the Gentile believers.
Connect the inclusion of Gentiles to OT prophecy (Amos 9).
Explain the concept of Christian Liberty vs. stumbling blocks.
Construct an argument for Salvation by Grace Alone using Acts 15.
Evaluate the significance of this moment for the global church.
Defend the unity of the church across ethnic lines.
Synthesize the transition from the Mosaic Law to the Law of Christ.

BIB.8.2.1.t: Identify that we listen to stories to learn about Jesus.
Name the Bible as a letter from God to us.
Recall that we should do what the Bible says.
Ask 'What does this teach me about God?'
Summarize the difference between what it meant then and what it means now.
Explain that context (what comes before and after) is important.
Compare a letter (Epistle) with a story (Gospel).
Apply the principle of letting Scripture interpret Scripture.
Analyze a passage using Observation, Interpretation, and Application.
Interpret parables differently than historical narrative.
Connect the cultural background to the meaning of a text.
Explain the danger of taking verses out of context.
Construct an exegetical outline of a passage.
Evaluate different interpretations using hermeneutical principles.
Defend the perspicuity (clarity) of Scripture for essential doctrines.
Synthesize the grammatical-historical method of interpretation.

BIB.8.2.2.t: Identify the Temple as the special place where people went to pray.
Name the land where Jesus lived as Israel.
Recall that Jewish people were waiting for a Rescuer.
Observe that they read the Old Testament scrolls.
Summarize the difference between the Temple and a Synagogue.
Explain who the Pharisees and Sadducees were.
Compare the Jewish people's desire for a King with Jesus' arrival.
Locate Judea, Samaria, and Galilee on a map.
Analyze the political tension between the Jews and Romans.
Interpret the significance of the 'Second Temple' period.
Connect the dispersion (Diaspora) of Jews to the spread of the Gospel.
Explain the messianic expectations of the first century.
Construct a profile of the major Jewish sects (Essenes, Zealots, Pharisees, Sadducees).
Evaluate the influence of Hellenism (Greek culture) on Judaism.
Perform research on the works of Josephus.
Synthesize the religious climate that prepared the way for Christ.

BIB.8.2.3.t: Identify the New Testament as God's Word.
Name the Apostles as the men who wrote the books.
Recall that the Bible is true and special.
Observe that the books are collected into one big book.
Summarize how we got the 27 books of the NT.
Explain that 'Canon' means a measuring stick or rule.
Compare Scripture with other good Christian books.
Categorize the books by author (Paul, John, Peter, etc.).

Interpret the role of the Holy Spirit in preserving Scripture.
Connect the early church councils to the recognition of the books.
Explain why the Gnostic gospels were rejected.
Construct a defense of the closed canon.
Evaluate the Muratorian Fragment and other early lists.
Defend the reliability of the textual transmission of the NT.
Produce a study on the self-attesting nature of Scripture.

BIB.8.2.4.t: Identify that there was a long quiet time before Jesus came.
Name 400 years as the time between the Testaments.
Recall that people were waiting and praying.
Observe that God was still working even when He was silent.
Summarize why it is called the 'Silent Years' (no prophets).
Explain the story of the Maccabees and Hanukkah.
Compare the Persian Empire (end of OT) with the Roman Empire (start of NT).
Categorize the major empires between Malachi and Matthew (Greek, Roman).
Analyze the impact of Alexander the Great on biblical history.
Interpret the 'Abomination of Desolation' by Antiochus Epiphanes.
Connect the Septuagint (Greek OT) to the New Testament writers.
Explain the rise of the synagogue system.
Construct a timeline of the Intertestamental Period.
Evaluate the Apocrypha as historical background versus inspired Scripture.
Defend the continuity of God's plan during the silent years.
Produce an essay on how this period set the stage for the 'fullness of time' (Gal 4:4).

BIB.8.2.5.t: Identify Roman soldiers by their armor.
Name Caesar as the boss of the Roman Empire.
Recall that Romans built big roads.
Observe a coin that Jesus might have used.
Explain why tax collectors were hated.
Compare the Roman governor (Pilate) with the Jewish King (Herod).
Apply the concept of common language (Greek) helping missionaries.
Analyze the benefits of Roman infrastructure for the Gospel.

Connect Roman law and citizenship to Paul's ministry.
Explain the social hierarchy of the Roman world (citizens vs slaves).
Construct a map of the Roman Empire's provinces.
Evaluate the conflict between 'Jesus is Lord' and 'Caesar is Lord'.
Perform research on the patronage system in Roman society.
Synthesize the political environment of the Gospels and Acts.

BIB.8.3.1.t: Name Jesus walking among the lampstands.
Recall that Jesus knows what we do.
Summarize the commendation and rebuke pattern.
Compare the suffering church (Smyrna) with the dead church (Sardis).
Analyze the historical context of each city.
Connect the local struggles to universal church issues.
Explain the symbol of the lampstand (witness).
Construct a spiritual health check based on the seven letters.
Evaluate the relevance of these warnings today.
Defend the authority of Christ over His church.

BIB.8.3.2.t: Identify the Lamb and the Lion.
Name the Dragon as the enemy.
Recall that numbers mean things (7 = perfect).
Observe strange creatures with eyes and wings.
Summarize the vision of the Throne Room (Rev 4).
Explain why Jesus is called the Lamb who was slain.
Compare the Beast with the Lamb.
Analyze the use of Daniel and Ezekiel in Revelation.
Interpret the meaning of 'Babylon' as the world system.
Connect the plagues to the Exodus.
Explain the Mark of the Beast vs. the Seal of God.
Construct a guide to biblical numerology.
Evaluate literal vs. symbolic interpretation methods.
Defend the genre of Apocalyptic as distinct from narrative.
Synthesize the cosmic conflict between the Seed of the Woman and the Serpent.

BIB.8.3.3.t: Recall that Satan is thrown away forever.
Summarize the Marriage Supper of the Lamb.
Compare the temporary power of evil with the eternal power of God.
Connect the Great White Throne to justice.
Construct a timeline of the Last Days (according to a specific view or comparing views).
Evaluate the comfort this brings to persecuted Christians.
Defend the physical return of Christ.
Synthesize the vindication of God's holiness.

BIB.8.3.4.t: Recall that God will live with us.
Observe that there is no sun because God is the light.
Summarize 'Behold, I make all things new'.
Explain that there is no more crying or pain.
Compare the Garden of Eden with the Garden City.
Identify the Tree of Life (healing of nations).
Analyze the dimensions of the city (Holy of Holies).
Interpret the absence of a Temple.
Connect the Bride imagery to the Church.
Explain the beatific vision (seeing His face).
Construct a description of Heaven based on Scripture.
Evaluate popular myths about heaven (clouds/harps) vs. biblical reality (New Earth).
Defend the physical nature of the resurrection state.
Synthesize the teleology of creation (God all in all).

BIB.8.4.1.t: Identify James as the brother of Jesus.
Name the tongue as a small spark.

Identify wisdom from above vs. below.

BIB.8.4.2.t: Identify Peter as the disciple who denied Jesus but was restored.
